papers.title_zh: lncRNA ZNF667-AS1通过调节miR-210-3p上调CPEB2抑制乙型肝炎病毒相关肝细胞癌
papers.source_body_en: To explore the biological functions, clinical significance, and regulatory mechanism of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) ZNF667-AS1 in hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). One hundred and seven patients with HBV-related HCC, one hundred and five patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and one hundred and five healthy controls were enrolled in this study. Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) was used to detect the expression levels of ZNF667-AS1, miR-210-3p, CPEB2. The association between ZNF667-AS1 expression and clinical characteristics of patients were analyzed, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate its diagnostic value. Bioinformatics prediction and dual-luciferase reporter assays were conducted to verify the targeted associations between ZNF667-AS1 and miR-210-3p, as well as between miR-210-3p and CPEB2. Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) and Transwell assays were applied to assess the biological functions of HCC cells after cell transfection. The expression levels of ZNF667-AS1 and CPEB2 were significantly downregulated in tissue samples from patients with HBV-related HCC and in HBV-associated HCC cell lines. ROC curve analysis showed the area under the curve (AUC) of ZNF667-AS1 for diagnosing HBV-related HCC from CHB reached 0.841. miR-210-3p was validated as a direct target of ZNF667-AS1, and a significant negative correlation was observed between their expression levels. Overexpression of ZNF667-AS1 inhibited the proliferation, migration, and invasion of HCC cells, whereas this inhibitory effect was reversed by transfection with miR-210-3p mimic. LncRNA ZNF667-AS1 is downregulated in HBV-related HCC and exerts in vitro tumor‐suppressive effects by targeting miR-210-3p to upregulate CPEB2 expression, thus providing a potential auxiliary biomarker for HBV-related HCC diagnosis and a novel regulatory axis for understanding disease pathogenesis.
papers.abstract_zh: 探讨长链非编码RNA(lncRNA)ZNF667-AS1在乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)相关肝细胞癌(HCC)中的生物学功能、临床意义和调控机制。本研究纳入了 107 名 HBV 相关 HCC 患者、105 名 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 患者和 105 名健康对照者。采用实时定量聚合酶链反应(RT-qPCR)检测ZNF667-AS1、miR-210-3p、CPEB2的表达水平。分析ZNF667-AS1表达与患者临床特征的关联,并进行受试者工作特征(ROC)曲线分析以评估其诊断价值。进行生物信息学预测和双荧光素酶报告基因测定,以验证 ZNF667-AS1 和 miR-210-3p 之间以及 miR-210-3p 和 CPEB2 之间的靶向关联。应用细胞计数试剂盒-8 (CCK-8) 和 Transwell 检测来评估细胞转染后 HCC 细胞的生物学功能。在 HBV 相关 HCC 患者的组织样本和 HBV 相关 HCC 细胞系中,ZNF667-AS1 和 CPEB2 的表达水平显着下调。ROC曲线分析显示,ZNF667-AS1诊断CHB与HBV相关HCC的曲线下面积(AUC)达到0.841。miR-210-3p被验证为ZNF667-AS1的直接靶标,并且观察到它们的表达水平之间存在显着的负相关。ZNF667-AS1 的过表达抑制 HCC 细胞的增殖、迁移和侵袭,而这种抑制作用可通过转染 miR-210-3p 模拟物而逆转。LncRNA ZNF667-AS1 在 HBV 相关 HCC 中下调,并通过靶向 miR-210-3p 上调 CPEB2 表达发挥体外肿瘤抑制作用,从而为 HBV 相关 HCC 诊断 提供潜在的辅助生物标志物,并为理解疾病 诊断 提供新的调控轴。

papers.title: Diagnostic performance of liver biochemical and hemostatic markers for assessing cirrhosis severity in chronic hepatitis B
papers.abstract: This study aimed to explore the utility of liver biochemical and hemostatic (including coagulation, anticoagulation, and fibrinolysis) markers for assessing cirrhosis severity in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) patients. In this current study, a total of 28 healthy controls and 78 patients with CHB-related cirrhosis were enrolled. Routine laboratory markers including platelet count (PLT), albumin (ALB), total bilirubin (TBIL), creatinine (CREA), prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), factor VIII (FVIII), prothrombin activity (PA), protein S (PS), protein C (PC), antithrombin III (AT-III) and D-dimer (D-D) were measured. Correlations between the measured parameters and Child-Pugh score (CPS)/ Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score (MELD) were also explored. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the ability of these indicators to discriminate between mild and moderate-to-severe CHB-related cirrhosis. Patients with CHB-related cirrhosis exhibited significantly lower levels of ALB, PA, PS, PC, AT-III, and PLT, and significantly higher levels of TBIL, PT, APTT, FVIII, and D-D, compared with healthy controls ( p < 0.05). ALB, PA, AT-III, PS, and PC showed significant negative correlations with both CPS and MELD ( p < 0.01). TBIL, PT, and APTT demonstrated significant positive correlations ( p < 0.01). ROC curve analysis revealed that AT-III achieved an AUC of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.88–1.00) for distinguishing cirrhosis severity, followed by PC (AUC: 0.87) and PA (AUC: 0.87). As expected, Child-Pugh components (ALB, TBIL, PT) showed strong associations with the score. Among markers not incorporated into the CPS, AT-III is significantly associated with the severity of CHB-related cirrhosis and exhibits promising discriminatory ability for staging CHB-related cirrhosis. It may support a low-cost, objective framework for dynamic monitoring of HBV-related cirrhosis progression. Although ALB, TBIL, and PT were also correlated with disease severity, these associations are subject to incorporation bias and thus represent confirmatory rather than novel findings.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) leads to cirrhosis, but noninvasive markers for assessing its severity are limited. This study asked whether liver biochemical and hemostatic markers can objectively stage CHB-related cirrhosis.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study enrolled 28 healthy controls and 78 patients with CHB-related cirrhosis to evaluate diagnostic markers.
analysis.methods: Routine laboratory markers including platelet count, albumin, total bilirubin, creatinine, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII, prothrombin activity, protein S, protein C, antithrombin III and D-dimer were measured. Correlations with Child-Pugh and MELD scores were explored, and ROC curve analysis assessed discrimination between mild and moderate-to-severe cirrhosis.
analysis.main_results: Patients with CHB-related cirrhosis had significantly lower albumin, prothrombin activity, protein S, protein C, antithrombin III and platelet count, and significantly higher total bilirubin, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII and D-dimer than healthy controls (p < 0.05). Antithrombin III showed the highest area under the ROC curve (0.95, 95% CI 0.88–1.00) for distinguishing cirrhosis severity, followed by protein C and prothrombin activity (each AUC 0.87).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Antithrombin III was significantly associated with CHB-related cirrhosis severity and showed strong discriminatory ability for staging, whereas albumin, total bilirubin and prothrombin time associations reflected incorporation bias and were confirmatory rather than novel.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest antithrombin III could enable low-cost, objective monitoring of HBV-related cirrhosis progression in clinical practice.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The cross-sectional design and small sample limit causal inference and generalisability; evidence strength is moderate due to potential selection bias and unadjusted confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study evaluated whether liver biochemical and hemostatic markers can stage cirrhosis severity in 78 patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB)-related cirrhosis and 28 healthy controls. Routine markers including albumin, prothrombin activity, protein S, protein C, antithrombin III, platelet count, total bilirubin, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII and D-dimer were measured. Patients with cirrhosis showed significantly lower levels of albumin, prothrombin activity, protein S, protein C, antithrombin III and platelet count, and higher levels of total bilirubin, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII and D-dimer than controls. Antithrombin III achieved the highest area under the ROC curve (0.95) for distinguishing cirrhosis severity, followed by protein C and prothrombin activity (each 0.87). The authors interpret antithrombin III as a promising marker for staging CHB-related cirrhosis, while noting that associations of albumin, total bilirubin and prothrombin time reflect incorporation bias. The study suggests antithrombin III could support low-cost, objective monitoring of HBV-related cirrhosis progression.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) leads to cirrhosis, but noninvasive markers for assessing its severity are limited. This study asked whether liver biochemical and hemostatic markers can objectively stage CHB-related cirrhosis.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study enrolled 28 healthy controls and 78 patients with CHB-related cirrhosis to evaluate diagnostic markers.
analysis_en.methods: Routine laboratory markers including platelet count, albumin, total bilirubin, creatinine, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII, prothrombin activity, protein S, protein C, antithrombin III and D-dimer were measured. Correlations with Child-Pugh and MELD scores were explored, and ROC curve analysis assessed discrimination between mild and moderate-to-severe cirrhosis.
analysis_en.main_results: Patients with CHB-related cirrhosis had significantly lower albumin, prothrombin activity, protein S, protein C, antithrombin III and platelet count, and significantly higher total bilirubin, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII and D-dimer than healthy controls (p < 0.05). papers.title_zh: 慢性乙型肝炎 肝脏生化和止血标志物评估肝硬化严重程度的诊断性能
papers.source_body_en: This study aimed to explore the utility of liver biochemical and hemostatic (including coagulation, anticoagulation, and fibrinolysis) markers for assessing cirrhosis severity in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) patients. In this current study, a total of 28 healthy controls and 78 patients with CHB-related cirrhosis were enrolled. Routine laboratory markers including platelet count (PLT), albumin (ALB), total bilirubin (TBIL), creatinine (CREA), prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), factor VIII (FVIII), prothrombin activity (PA), protein S (PS), protein C (PC), antithrombin III (AT-III) and D-dimer (D-D) were measured. Correlations between the measured parameters and Child-Pugh score (CPS)/ Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score (MELD) were also explored. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the ability of these indicators to discriminate between mild and moderate-to-severe CHB-related cirrhosis. Patients with CHB-related cirrhosis exhibited significantly lower levels of ALB, PA, PS, PC, AT-III, and PLT, and significantly higher levels of TBIL, PT, APTT, FVIII, and D-D, compared with healthy controls ( p < 0.05). ALB, PA, AT-III, PS, and PC showed significant negative correlations with both CPS and MELD ( p < 0.01). TBIL, PT, and APTT demonstrated significant positive correlations ( p < 0.01). ROC curve analysis revealed that AT-III achieved an AUC of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.88–1.00) for distinguishing cirrhosis severity, followed by PC (AUC: 0.87) and PA (AUC: 0.87). As expected, Child-Pugh components (ALB, TBIL, PT) showed strong associations with the score. Among markers not incorporated into the CPS, AT-III is significantly associated with the severity of CHB-related cirrhosis and exhibits promising discriminatory ability for staging CHB-related cirrhosis. It may support a low-cost, objective framework for dynamic monitoring of HBV-related cirrhosis progression. Although ALB, TBIL, and PT were also correlated with disease severity, these associations are subject to incorporation bias and thus represent confirmatory rather than novel findings.
papers.abstract_zh: 本研究旨在探讨肝脏生化和止血(包括凝血、抗凝和纤溶)标志物在评估 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 患者肝硬化严重程度方面的效用。在本研究中,共有 28 名健康对照者和 78 名患有 CHB 相关肝硬化的患者入组。测量常规实验室指标,包括血小板计数(PLT)、白蛋白(ALB)、总胆红素(TBIL)、肌酐(CREA)、凝血酶原时间(PT)、活化部分凝血活酶时间(APTT)、因子VIII(FVIII)、凝血酶原活性(PA)、蛋白S(PS)、蛋白C(PC)、抗凝血酶III(AT-III)和D-二聚体(D-D)。还探讨了测量参数与 Child-Pugh 评分 (CPS)/终末期肝病模型评分 (MELD) 之间的相关性。进行受试者工作特征 (ROC) 曲线分析,以评估这些指标区分轻度和中度至重度 CHB 相关肝硬化的能力。与健康对照相比,CHB 相关肝硬化患者的 ALB、PA、PS、PC、AT-III 和 PLT 水平显着降低,而 TBIL、PT、APTT、FVIII 和 D-D 水平显着升高 (p < 0.05)。ALB、PA、AT-III、PS 和 PC 与 CPS 和 MELD 均呈显着负相关 (p < 0.01)。TBIL、PT 和 APTT 表现出显着的正相关性 (p < 0.01)。ROC曲线分析显示,AT-III区分肝硬化严重程度的AUC为0.95(95% CI:0.88-1.00),其次是PC(AUC:0.87)和PA(AUC:0.87)。正如预期的那样,Child-Pugh 成分(ALB、TBIL、PT)与分数显示出很强的关联性。在未纳入 CPS 的标志物中,AT-III 与 CHB 相关肝硬化的严重程度显着相关,并且在 CHB 相关肝硬化分期方面表现出有希望的区分能力。它可能支持动态监测 HBV 相关肝硬化进展的低成本、客观框架。尽管 ALB、TBIL 和 PT 也与疾病严重程度相关,但这些关联会受到合并偏倚的影响,因此代表的是证实性而非新颖的发现。

papers.title: CXCL16 gene promoter methylation is associated with inflammation in patients with chronic hepatitis B
papers.abstract: Abstract Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection causes persistent hepatic inflammation, and chemokine CXCL16 serves as a key mediator in liver injury, but its epigenetic regulation in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains unclear. This study enrolled 217 CHB patients (113 HBeAg‐positive, 104 HBeAg‐negative) and 27 healthy controls to investigate CXCL16 promoter methylation, mRNA and protein expression, as well as their correlations with inflammatory indices and liver injury markers. The results showed that CXCL16 promoter methylation was significantly lower, while CXCL16 mRNA and serum levels were markedly higher in CHB patients, especially in HBeAg‐positive cases. CXCL16 promoter methylation was negatively correlated with CXCL16 expression, HBeAg status, ALT, AST, TNF‐α and IL‐1βlevels. ROC analysis indicated that CXCL16 promoter methylation had favorable diagnostic value for evaluating hepatic inflammatory injury in CHB patients. In conclusion, CXCL16 promoter hypomethylation is closely associated with elevated CXCL16 expression and exacerbated hepatic inflammation in CHB patients, and may serve as a potential non‐invasive biomarker for assessing CHB‐related liver inflammation. These findings enrich the epigenetic mechanism underlying HBV‐related hepatic inflammation and provide a novel target which is CXCL16 for clinical evaluation and intervention.

papers.title: Biopsy-Based Head-to-Head Comparison of Eight Non-Invasive Fibrosis Scores in Treatment-Naïve Chronic Hepatitis B
papers.abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Accurate fibrosis staging is essential for managing chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Although several non-invasive fibrosis scores have been proposed as alternatives to liver biopsy, their comparative performance across fibrosis stages remains uncertain. This study compared eight commonly used non-invasive fibrosis scores for detecting significant, advanced, and severe fibrosis in treatment-naïve patients with CHB. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included treatment-naïve patients with CHB who underwent liver biopsy between May 2017 and May 2024. Fibrosis was staged using the Ishak scoring system. APRI, FIB-4, KING, GUCI, AAR, API, INPR, and GPR were evaluated for detecting F ≥ 2, F ≥ 3, and F ≥ 4 fibrosis using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Optimal cut-off values were determined using the Youden index. AUROC, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were calculated. Pairwise AUROC comparisons were performed using DeLong's test. Results A total of 268 patients were included. All scores showed poor performance for detecting significant fibrosis (F ≥ 2), with AUROC values below 0.60. Diagnostic accuracy improved for advanced and severe fibrosis. KING achieved the highest AUROC for advanced fibrosis (0.807), followed by FIB-4 (0.797), whereas GPR showed the highest AUROC for severe fibrosis (0.929). DeLong analysis demonstrated no significant differences among the best-performing scores. Conclusion None of the evaluated scores demonstrated sufficient accuracy to replace liver biopsy for detecting significant fibrosis. However, FIB-4, KING, and GPR showed good performance for advanced and severe fibrosis and may be useful for initial risk stratification and identifying patients who require further evaluation with liver biopsy.

papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 背景和目的 准确的纤维化分期对于治疗 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 至关重要。尽管已提出几种非侵入性纤维化评分作为肝活检的替代方法,但它们在纤维化阶段的比较表现仍不确定。这项研究比较了八种常用的非侵入性纤维化评分,用于检测 治疗 初治慢性乙型肝炎患者的显着、晚期和严重纤维化。材料和方法 这项回顾性研究纳入了 2017 年 5 月至 2024 年 5 月期间接受肝活检的 治疗 初治慢性乙型肝炎患者。使用 Ishak 评分系统对纤维化进行分期。使用接受者操作特征 (ROC) 分析评估 APRI、FIB-4、KING、GUCI、AAR、API、INPR 和 GPR 检测 F ≥ 2、F ≥ 3 和 F ≥ 4 纤维化的情况。使用约登指数确定最佳截止值。计算AUROC、敏感性、特异性、阳性预测值和阴性预测值。使用 DeLong 检验进行成对 AUROC 比较。结果共纳入268例患者。所有评分在检测显着纤维化(F ≥ 2)方面表现不佳,AUROC 值低于 0.60。晚期和严重纤维化的诊断准确性得到提高。KING 在晚期纤维化方面取得了最高的 AUROC (0.807),其次是 FIB-4 (0.797),而 GPR 在严重纤维化方面取得了最高的 AUROC (0.929)。德隆分析表明,表现最好的分数之间没有显着差异。结论 评估的评分均未表现出足够的准确性来替代肝活检来检测显着的纤维化。然而,FIB-4、KING 和 GPR 在晚期和严重纤维化方面表现出良好的性能,可能有助于初步风险分层和识别需要肝活检进一步评估的患者。

analysis_zh.methods: 使用 Ishak 评分系统对纤维化进行分期,并使用 ROC 分析评估八种非侵入性纤维化评分(APRI、FIB-4、KING、GUCI、AAR、API、INPR、GPR)以检测 F ≥ 2、F ≥ 3 和 F ≥ 4 纤维化,最佳截止值由 Youden 指数确定。
analysis_zh.main_results: 总共纳入268名患者;所有评分在检测显着纤维化 (F ≥ 2) 方面表现不佳,AUROC 值低于 0.60,但晚期和严重纤维化的诊断准确性有所提高,KING 在晚期纤维化方面取得了最高的 AUROC (0.807),在严重纤维化方面取得了最高的 GPR (0.929)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出的结论是,尽管 FIB-4、KING 和 GPR 在检测晚期和严重纤维化方面表现出良好的性能,但所有评估的评分都没有表现出足够的准确性来替代肝活检来检测显着的纤维化。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: FIB-4、KING 和 GPR 可能有助于初步风险分层和识别需要肝活检进一步评估的患者,从而可能减少临床实践中不必要的活检。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是回顾性的,仅限于 治疗 初治患者,由于单中心设计和依赖活检作为参考标准,证据强度评估为中等。

Chronic infections such as hepatitis B and C may negatively affect patients’ sexual well-being through both biological mechanisms and emotional distress related to stigma and fear of transmission. Despite this, limited research has addressed how a hepatitis diagnosis influences sexual behavior and satisfaction, particularly from a primary care perspective. elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该研究采用观察分析设计,对象是被诊断患有乙型和丙型肝炎感染的患者群体。使用评估社会人口特征和性行为的调查问卷以及 Golombok Rust 性满意度清单收集数据。

elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该研究发现阴道性交频率的下降与教育水平有关,但所提供的证据并未报告具体的统计细节或 p 值。从初级保健的角度来看,关于 诊断 肝炎如何影响性行为和满意度的研究有限。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 需要进一步的研究来解决对肝炎对性行为和满意度的影响的有限理解,特别是从初级保健的角度来看。研究结果强调需要采取干预措施来解决肝炎患者的性健康和伴侣焦虑问题。

papers.title: Hepatitis Prevalence Among Key Populations in Nigeria: A Scoping Review
papers.abstract: Nigeria faces a high burden of viral hepatitis, with key populations (KPs) such as sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender people, people who inject drugs (PWIDs), and people in prisons. The study aims to review existing evidence on hepatitis among KPs in Nigeria, evaluate study quality, highlight knowledge gaps, and guide public health policy. We conducted a scoping review following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Six databases and gray literature were searched for studies on hepatitis prevalence among KPs in Nigeria (2008–2025). Two independent reviewers screened and extracted data, and study quality was assessed using adapted Joanna Briggs Institute criteria. From 1,270 records screened, 25 studies were included, covering five KP groups in 12 Nigerian states. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) prevalence ranged from 4.0% among sex workers in Enugu to 23.0% in prisons, with MSM and transgender people showing 10.0% in Abuja and Lagos. PWID recorded 6.6– 7.8% HBV and 2.3–3.3% hepatitis C virus (HCV) prevalence, while prisons carried the highest burden. Northern Nigeria showed major data gaps despite higher population prevalence. Methodological weaknesses were found in 68% of studies, with limited evidence for HCV (32%), transgender populations (12%), and rural groups (8%). KPs in Nigeria, particularly prisoners, face a higher hepatitis burden than the general population. There are major evidence gaps on HCV, transgender groups, and rural areas, highlighting the need for more research, wider surveillance, and integrated human immunodeficiency virus-hepatitis services.

papers.abstract_zh: 尼日利亚面临着沉重的病毒性肝炎负担,其重点人群(KP)包括性工作者、男男性行为者(MSM)、跨性别者、注射吸毒者(PWID)和监狱人员。该研究旨在审查尼日利亚 KP 肝炎的现有证据,评估研究质量,突出知识差距并指导公共卫生政策。我们按照 Arksey 和 O’Malley 框架以及系统评价的首选报告项目和范围界定审查指南的元分析扩展进行了范围界定审查。检索了六个数据库和灰色文献,查找了尼日利亚 KP 中肝炎 患病率 的研究(2008-2025 年)。两名独立评审员筛选并提取数据,并使用改编后的乔安娜·布里格斯研究所标准评估研究质量。从筛选的 1,270 份记录中纳入了 25 项研究,涵盖尼日利亚 12 个州的 5 个 KP 团体。乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV) 患病率 的比例从埃努古性工作者的 4.0% 到监狱中的 23.0%,而阿布贾和拉各斯的 MSM 和跨性别者则为 10.0%。注射吸毒者的乙肝病毒感染率为 6.6-7.8%,丙型肝炎病毒 (HCV) 患病率 感染率为 2.3-3.3%,而监狱的负担最高。尽管 患病率 人口较多,但尼日利亚北部仍显示出重大数据差距。68% 的研究发现方法学上的缺陷,丙肝病毒 (32%)、变性人群 (12%) 和农村群体 (8%) 的证据有限。尼日利亚的 KP,特别是囚犯,面临着比一般人群更高的肝炎负担。HCV、跨性别群体和农村地区存在重大证据差距,凸显需要进行更多研究、更广泛的 监测 以及人类免疫缺陷病毒-肝炎综合服务。

analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 根据 Arksey 和 O'Malley 框架和 PRISMA-ScR 指南进行了范围界定审查,检索了 2008 年至 2025 年的六个数据库和灰色文献。两名独立评审员筛选了 1,270 份记录,纳入了涵盖尼日利亚 12 个州的 5 个 KP 小组的 25 项研究,并使用改编后的乔安娜·布里格斯研究所标准评估了研究质量。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: KP 中的 HBV 患病率 差异显着,从性工作者 (Enugu) 的 4.0% 到监狱中的 23.0%,而阿布贾和拉各斯的 MSM 和跨性别者则为 10.0%。注射吸毒者的 HBV 患病率 记录为 6.6–7.8%。KP,特别是囚犯,面临着比一般人群更高的肝炎负担。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 主要证据差距存在于尼日利亚北部、HCV 研究(占研究的 32%)、变性人群(12%)和农村群体(8%)。68% 的研究发现方法学上的缺陷,限制了研究结果的可靠性。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 迫切需要对 HCV、跨性别人群和农村地区进行更多研究,同时扩大 监测 和综合艾滋病毒肝炎服务,以解决尼日利亚 KP 的不成比例的负担。

papers.title: Diagnostic capacity and utilization of Hepatitis B and C testing across multiple health care sectors in Vietnam
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The WHO aims to eliminate hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) as public health threats by 2030, yet diagnosis remains suboptimal in many low- and middle-income countries. Access to diagnostics is often emphasized, but how far existing capacity is used is poorly characterized. We quantified installed capacity and utilization of HBV/HCV testing across three primary-care–linked Vietnamese facilities and described disease stage. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional inventory and utilization audit of serologic (HBsAg, anti-HCV) and molecular (HBV DNA, HCV RNA) testing during 2018–2020 at a private diagnostic network, a public district hospital, and a teaching/research institute. Utilization was tests performed divided by maximum theoretical capacity. Facility-level data on fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) at diagnosis were drawn from routine records. Results In 2019 (pre-COVID-19 reference year), serologic and PCR utilization were 50.0% and 18.8% at the private network, 5.0% and 21.3% at the public hospital, and lowest at the teaching institute (3.5% and 3.0%). Advanced fibrosis (≥ F3) rose over 2018–2020 from 11.4% to 16.6% in HBV and 21.6% to 37.5% in HCV. Most HCC occurred in individuals with HBV infection (52.3% and 21.4% at the two larger sites) and coexisted with high unused capacity; we did not assess testing accuracy. Conclusions Substantial HBV/HCV diagnostic infrastructure exists in Vietnam but is unevenly used. Because data were facility-aggregated, these are associations, not patient-level causal relationships. Optimizing use of existing platforms may help address systemic inefficiencies and support elimination efforts.

analysis.methods: Utilization was calculated as tests performed divided by maximum theoretical capacity, and facility-level data on fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) at diagnosis were drawn from routine records.
analysis.main_results: In 2019 (pre-COVID-19 reference year), serologic and PCR utilization were 50.0% and 18.8% at the private network, 5.0% and 21.3% at the public hospital, and lowest at the teaching institute (3.5% and 3.0%). analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated diagnostic capacity and utilization for hepatitis B and C across three Vietnamese healthcare facilities. The WHO aims to eliminate HBV and HCV by 2030, but diagnosis remains suboptimal in many low- and middle-income countries. Researchers conducted a cross-sectional audit of serologic and molecular testing from 2018-2020, finding substantial but unevenly used diagnostic infrastructure. In 2019, utilization rates varied widely: 50.0% serologic and 18.8% PCR at the private network, compared to 5.0% and 21.3% at the public hospital, and 3.5% and 3.0% at the teaching institute. Advanced fibrosis increased over time, and most HCC cases occurred in HBV-infected individuals despite high unused capacity. The study suggests optimizing existing platforms could address inefficiencies and support elimination efforts, though facility-aggregated data limit causal inferences.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 世界卫生组织的目标是到 2030 年消除 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV) 和丙型肝炎病毒 (HCV) 作为公共卫生威胁,但 诊断 在许多低收入和中等收入国家仍然不理想。人们经常强调获得诊断的机会,但现有能力的使用程度却很少被描述。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们在 2018 年至 2020 年期间对越南的一家私人诊断网络、一家公立地区医院和一家教学/研究机构进行了血清学(HBsAg、抗 HCV)和分子(HBV DNA、HCV RNA)检测的横断面库存和使用审核。
elements_zh.methods: 利用率的计算方法是进行的测试除以最大理论容量,并从常规记录中提取 诊断 的纤维化、肝硬化和肝细胞癌 (HCC) 设施级数据。
elements_zh.main_results: 2019 年(COVID-19 之前的参考年),私人网络的血清学和 PCR 利用率分别为 50.0% 和 18.8%,公立医院为 5.0% 和 21.3%,教学机构最低(3.5% 和 3.0%)。2018 年至 2020 年期间,乙肝病毒中的晚期纤维化(≥ F3)从 11.4% 上升至 16.6%,丙肝病毒中的晚期纤维化从 21.6% 上升至 37.5%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 越南拥有大量的 HBV/HCV 诊断基础设施,但使用不均衡。大多数 HCC 发生在 HBV 感染个体中(两个较大地点分别为 52.3% 和 21.4%),并且与大量未使用容量并存。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 优化现有平台的使用可能有助于解决系统效率低下的问题并支持消除工作。研究结果强调需要提高诊断能力的利用率以减少晚期肝病。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于数据是按机构汇总的,因此这些是关联,而不是患者层面的因果关系。由于横截面设计和缺乏测试准确性评估,证据强度中等。

Results In 2019 (pre-COVID-19 reference year), serologic and PCR utilization were 50.0% and 18.8% at the private network, 5.0% and 21.3% at the public hospital, and lowest at the teaching institute (3.5% and 3.0%). Advanced fibrosis (≥ F3) rose over 2018–2020 from 11.4% to 16.6% in HBV and 21.6% to 37.5% in HCV. Most HCC occurred in individuals with HBV infection (52.3% and 21.4% at the two larger sites) and coexisted with high unused capacity; we did not assess testing accuracy. Conclusions Substantial HBV/HCV diagnostic infrastructure exists in Vietnam but is unevenly used. Because data were facility-aggregated, these are associations, not patient-level causal relationships. Optimizing use of existing platforms may help address systemic inefficiencies and support elimination efforts.

papers.title: The Use of Forward Chaining for Early Detection of Hepatitis B Risk Among Pregnant Women at Beber Community Health Center, Cirebon Regency
papers.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major public health problem in Indonesia, particularly among pregnant women, where delayed detection may increase the risk of mother-to-child transmission as well as serious complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. The high cost of laboratory testing may contribute to delays in diagnosis and treatment. This study aimed to design a web-based early detection system for hepatitis B in pregnant women using the Forward Chaining method. A mixed-methods approach with a Research and Development (R&D) design was employed to develop and evaluate the system. The developed system was tested on 30 respondents and achieved a 100% success rate in black-box testing. Validation results showed a sensitivity of 100%, specificity of 90%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 82%, negative predictive value (NPV) of 100%, and an accuracy of 93%, indicating good diagnostic performance. The developed system can assist in the early detection of hepatitis B among pregnant women and may support earlier identification of the risk of mother-to-child transmission in primary healthcare settings.

analysis.time: Event date: 27 Jul 2026 (Brazil's validation request). Publication date: 2026-07-29 (PAHO news release).
analysis.location_and_population: Brazil; general population, specifically mothers and infants involved in mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B.
analysis.event: Brazil is seeking validation of the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV) from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). The request is reported as a public health initiative but lacks specific confirmation details in the evidence.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Not reported in the supplied evidence. No case counts, deaths, or exposure figures provided. Risk level remains unspecified.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Under investigation/pending validation. PAHO is reviewing Brazil's claim, but no confirmation of elimination status or implementation steps is detailed in the evidence.

analysis.brief_en: On July 27, 2026, Brazil requested validation from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) regarding the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV). The PAHO news release on July 29, 2026, highlighted this initiative as part of broader regional health efforts but did not confirm Brazil's success or provide specific metrics. The request aligns with PAHO's focus on hepatitis B elimination in the Americas, though the evidence lacks details on case numbers, transmission rates, or public health interventions. This development reflects ongoing efforts to eradicate HBV in vulnerable populations, particularly infants, but remains unverified without additional data. The initiative is part of PAHO's strategic goals for hepatitis B control, yet its status remains under review.

news.content: AboutPeople/StaffAlumniLibraryVisit WitsGiveApply Homepage Study at WitsStudentsFaculties and SchoolsTeaching and LearningResearch and InnovationNews Search Search the site Search Menu Search Search the site Search Start main page content HomeNewsLatest newsResearch news2026 2026-07 Next-generation technologies take aim at hepatitis B 28 July 2026 - Wits University Four young scientists at AGTRU leverage vaccine science and gene therapy advances for novel treatment and prevention of hepatitis B. The students' projects at the Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit (AGTRU) address hepatitis B virus (HBV) at different stages, from strengthening protection against infection to targeting it once it has become chronic. As World Hepatitis Day is marked on 28 July, these projects show why HBV must be tackled at every stage, from preventing infection to disabling the virus once it has entered liver cells. This work is most urgent for babies and young children, and in high-burden regions such as Africa. In 2024, around 240 million people were living with chronic HBV, while 1.1 million died from related cirrhosis and liver cancer. Africa accounted for 68% of new chronic infections. The virus is particularly dangerous when acquired in infancy or early childhood because babies and young children are far less likely than adults to clear it. HBV infection may remain silent for years while continuing to damage the liver, eventually causing fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer. South Africa incorporated the highly effective hepatitis B vaccine into its childhood immunisation programme in 1995. However, coverage gaps remain, while around 5–10% of vaccinated people do not produce a sufficient protective antibody response. A vaccine that could do more with less AGTRU PhD student Nazia Samudh is developing an HBV vaccine using self-amplifying RNA, one of the emerging generation of RNA vaccine platforms. Like conventional mRNA, it gives cells temporary instructions to produce a harmless viral antigen that trains the immune system. Self-amplifying RNA can briefly make additional copies of that message inside the cell. This results in more antigen being produced from a relatively lower vaccine dose. Because more antigen may be produced from a smaller starting dose, the platform could reduce the amount of RNA needed and, potentially, the cost of vaccination. “Some of our main goals are to address non-responsiveness to current HBV vaccines and investigate whether we can reduce the number of doses required,” says Samudh. Currently, three doses are required, and Samudh aims to elicit sufficient protection with just two doses. Fewer clinic visits could make vaccination easier in communities where distance, cost and inconsistent access to healthcare make it difficult to complete a multi-dose schedule. Combining platforms for broader protection PhD student Keila Neves is testing an adenoviral-vector vaccine followed by an mRNA booster. “It’s not just a vaccine candidate; it’s an entire regimen,” says Neves. Samudh and Neves are also testing vaccine candidates that present more of HBV’s outer surface to the immune system. Existing vaccines mainly use the small hepatitis B surface antigen; their candidates incorporate additional regions from the virus’s larger surface proteins, potentially stimulating a broader immune response. The candidates are designed around HBV subgenotype A1, which predominates in southern Africa and is associated with an increased risk of liver cancer. Silencing the virus AGTRU Master’s student Pieter Jonker is developing a potential treatment for people already living with chronic HBV. Once HBV has infected a liver cell, it produces messenger RNA carrying the instructions needed to make viral proteins and new virus particles. Jonker is developing microRNA mimics that recognise and bind to these viral messages. By prompting the cell to destroy the messenger RNA or preventing it from being read, the treatment could reduce viral protein production and suppress replication. “We are generating a mimic of this microRNA that will bind to the virus’s messenger RNA, essentially stopping it from making more viruses,” he explains. Gene editing and “mini livers” AGTRU PhD student Tasneem Farhad is investigating whether CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing can recognise and disable persistent HBV DNA in liver cells. A modified adenoviral vector would deliver the gene-editing machinery to its target. She is also developing a three-dimensional model of chronic HBV infection. Ordinary mice do not naturally reproduce human HBV infection well, making it difficult to test potential treatments. “The idea is to grow liver cells as a ‘mini liver’, infect them with hepatitis B and model what the infection looks like in a human,” says Farhad. Such models could provide a better bridge between conventional cell experiments and later-stage studies. Share 0 2 Close ShareThis Copy and PasteChat with me Kudubot Reply in 10 seconds. analysis.time: Published on 28 July 2026, with research activities ongoing at the Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit (AGTRU).
analysis.location_and_population: Research conducted at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in South Africa, focusing on populations in high-burden regions such as Africa, particularly babies and young children.
analysis.event: Four young scientists at AGTRU are developing next-generation technologies for hepatitis B virus (HBV) treatment and prevention, including novel vaccines and gene therapies, as reported by Wits University.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In 2024, approximately 240 million people were living with chronic HBV, with 1.1 million deaths related to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Africa accounted for 68% of new chronic infections. The virus poses a higher risk when acquired in infancy or early childhood.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Research is ongoing, with projects addressing vaccine non-responsiveness, dose reduction, and chronic HBV treatment using microRNA mimics and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing. South Africa has incorporated the HBV vaccine into its childhood immunization program since 1995, but coverage gaps and non-responsiveness remain challenges.

analysis.brief_en: Wits University researchers are advancing next-generation technologies to combat hepatitis B virus (HBV), focusing on novel vaccines and treatments. Four scientists at the Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit (AGTRU) are developing self-amplifying RNA vaccines to reduce doses and costs, adenoviral-vector/mRNA boosters for broader protection, and microRNA mimics and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to target chronic infections. With 240 million chronic cases globally and 1.1 million annual deaths, Africa bears 68% of new infections. The research prioritizes high-risk groups like infants and children, addressing gaps in current vaccine coverage and non-responsiveness. These innovations aim to improve prevention and treatment in resource-limited settings.

analysis.event: Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF, Vemlidy) has been listed for hepatitis B virus treatment on provincial and federal formularies in Canada. This is a confirmed policy change.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: Not reported in the supplied evidence. Deaths: Not reported in the supplied evidence. Exposures: Not reported in the supplied evidence. The change improves access to treatment for people with hepatitis B, particularly those without private insurance.

analysis.brief_en: CATIE.ca reports that tenofovir alafenamide (TAF, Vemlidy) is now listed for hepatitis B virus treatment on provincial and federal formularies across Canada. This policy change addresses a critical access issue, as many people with hepatitis B cannot afford the drug without private insurance. The listing of TAF, a recommended treatment for hepatitis B, represents a significant step in improving treatment accessibility for affected populations in Canada. The information is based on a full report from CATIE.ca, Canada's source for HIV and hepatitis C information.

news.content_title: How Primary Care Can Close the Hepatitis B Testing Gap, With Cary James
news.content: As World Hepatitis Day highlights global testing gaps, an expert outlines how primary care can identify at-risk patients sooner. World Hepatitis Day falls each year on July 28, marking a global effort to close persistent gaps in hepatitis B diagnosis and care. A survey funded and commissioned by GSK, conducted online among approximately 5000 adults across Canada, Japan, Taiwan, China, and Germany, found that public understanding of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains strikingly limited. Among the 1061 Canadian adults aged 18 to 54 and older surveyed, only 31% rated CHB a high cancer risk, even though the virus accounts for up to 56% of liver cancer cases globally. Nearly 9 in 10 respondents reported being unaware or knowing very little about CHB, and 45% of Canadian adults said they have never been tested because they had not considered doing so or did not believe they were at risk. Among individuals considered at higher risk for CHB, nearly half said they do not intend to get tested, and separate findings show that 80% of at-risk individuals have never heard of CHB, with roughly 7 in 10 remaining untested. Misconceptions about prevention persist as well: 55% of Canadians incorrectly believe there is no treatment for CHB, and about 3 in 4 are unaware that vaccination offers protection. In the following Q&A, Cary James, CEO of World Hepatitis Alliance, discusses what this awareness gap means for how primary care clinicians should approach hepatitis B risk assessment and what practical steps can help normalize CHB testing during routine visits: Cary James: There's several ways in primary care to address this, right? You could have a protocol in place depending on how hepatitis B is manifested in that particular country. If there are certain populations that are more at risk, maybe certain migrant communities from high prevalence countries, first or second generation, or even key populations, you can put a protocol in if someone comes in for even a routine visit in primary care that they would be offered a hepatitis B test. This kind of comes back to whether those primary care physicians feel comfortable with doing that, or whether those people are familiar. It should just be routine. In most countries, hepatitis B tests are not that expensive, especially lab tests, so it should just be part of a general healthy living range of tests or things that are checked at least once in their life. In Germany, they have a policy that everyone should be tested at least once in their life. I think that is the protocol, and that would really make a huge difference. Sometimes, if you make an exception about something, then it makes it more scary. Streamlining it in primary care in the same way that they're talking about with HIV services in primary care. TB is talking about the same thing, like MDCV services. The main conversation about how we're going to solve the issues around decreased international funding in developing countries, but even in high income countries, is that things have to be evolved when they can in primary care, and hepatitis B is exactly the same. Cary James: I think it's kind of what I said before, right? If you know the communities in your catchment area of your clinic that may be affected by viral hepatitis, if you have some communities that are disproportionately affected, put some information in your waiting rooms. Talk to the patients about it during routine visits, and maybe put a protocol in place that all people from those communities are offered a test when they're also doing other kinds of routine tests. I think it's really important to normalize it as much as we can and take the stigma away from it. I think that once people know about it and know about the cancer risk, they want to get tested. They don't want to have something that they think might cause cancer. So, if you explain it in a way that's sort of like that, without prejudice, and this is just something that's important for you to know because no one wants to get cancer, then I think it's a much more appealing proposition than if you just talk about it as a singular concern. It is often associated with sexual transmission, which unfortunately still has lots of baggage on it around promiscuity and all kinds of stuff it doesn't deserve. I think the more you can normalize it and make the information available and make it part of the day-to-day care, the more applicants you'll get. Editors’ Note: Cary James is chief executive officer of the World Hepatitis Alliance. selected_identity.page_title: How Primary Care Can Close the Hepatitis B Testing Gap, With Cary James

news.content_original: As World Hepatitis Day highlights global testing gaps, an expert outlines how primary care can identify at-risk patients sooner. World Hepatitis Day falls each year on July 28, marking a global effort to close persistent gaps in hepatitis B diagnosis and care. A survey funded and commissioned by GSK, conducted online among approximately 5000 adults across Canada, Japan, Taiwan, China, and Germany, found that public understanding of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains strikingly limited. Among the 1061 Canadian adults aged 18 to 54 and older surveyed, only 31% rated CHB a high cancer risk, even though the virus accounts for up to 56% of liver cancer cases globally. Nearly 9 in 10 respondents reported being unaware or knowing very little about CHB, and 45% of Canadian adults said they have never been tested because they had not considered doing so or did not believe they were at risk. Among individuals considered at higher risk for CHB, nearly half said they do not intend to get tested, and separate findings show that 80% of at-risk individuals have never heard of CHB, with roughly 7 in 10 remaining untested. Misconceptions about prevention persist as well: 55% of Canadians incorrectly believe there is no treatment for CHB, and about 3 in 4 are unaware that vaccination offers protection. In the following Q&A, Cary James, CEO of World Hepatitis Alliance, discusses what this awareness gap means for how primary care clinicians should approach hepatitis B risk assessment and what practical steps can help normalize CHB testing during routine visits: Cary James: There's several ways in primary care to address this, right? You could have a protocol in place depending on how hepatitis B is manifested in that particular country. If there are certain populations that are more at risk, maybe certain migrant communities from high prevalence countries, first or second generation, or even key populations, you can put a protocol in if someone comes in for even a routine visit in primary care that they would be offered a hepatitis B test. This kind of comes back to whether those primary care physicians feel comfortable with doing that, or whether those people are familiar. It should just be routine. In most countries, hepatitis B tests are not that expensive, especially lab tests, so it should just be part of a general healthy living range of tests or things that are checked at least once in their life. In Germany, they have a policy that everyone should be tested at least once in their life. I think that is the protocol, and that would really make a huge difference. Sometimes, if you make an exception about something, then it makes it more scary. Streamlining it in primary care in the same way that they're talking about with HIV services in primary care. TB is talking about the same thing, like MDCV services. The main conversation about how we're going to solve the issues around decreased international funding in developing countries, but even in high income countries, is that things have to be evolved when they can in primary care, and hepatitis B is exactly the same. Cary James: I think it's kind of what I said before, right? If you know the communities in your catchment area of your clinic that may be affected by viral hepatitis, if you have some communities that are disproportionately affected, put some information in your waiting rooms. Talk to the patients about it during routine visits, and maybe put a protocol in place that all people from those communities are offered a test when they're also doing other kinds of routine tests. I think it's really important to normalize it as much as we can and take the stigma away from it. I think that once people know about it and know about the cancer risk, they want to get tested. They don't want to have something that they think might cause cancer. So, if you explain it in a way that's sort of like that, without prejudice, and this is just something that's important for you to know because no one wants to get cancer, then I think it's a much more appealing proposition than if you just talk about it as a singular concern. It is often associated with sexual transmission, which unfortunately still has lots of baggage on it around promiscuity and all kinds of stuff it doesn't deserve. I think the more you can normalize it and make the information available and make it part of the day-to-day care, the more applicants you'll get. Editors’ Note: Cary James is chief executive officer of the World Hepatitis Alliance. analysis.brief_en: This article discusses the persistent gaps in hepatitis B testing and awareness, particularly in chronic hepatitis B (CHB). A survey funded by GSK, conducted among approximately 5000 adults in Canada, Japan, Taiwan, China, and Germany, revealed that public understanding of CHB remains strikingly limited. In Canada, only 31% of 1061 adults surveyed rated CHB as a high cancer risk, even though it accounts for up to 56% of liver cancer cases globally. Nearly 90% of respondents were unaware or knew very little about CHB, and 45% of Canadian adults said they have never been tested because they had not considered doing so or did not believe they were at risk. The article highlights the importance of normalizing CHB testing in primary care settings, similar to HIV and TB testing, and suggests strategies such as offering tests during routine visits, educating communities, and reducing stigma. Cary James, CEO of the World Hepatitis Alliance, emphasizes the need for awareness campaigns and routine testing to address these gaps, especially in high-income countries where funding for hepatitis B is decreasing.

news.content_zh: 本文讨论了乙型肝炎检测和认识方面持续存在的差距,特别是在 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 领域。一项由 GSK 资助、针对加拿大、日本、台湾、中国和德国约 5000 名成年人进行的调查显示,公众对慢性乙型肝炎的了解仍然非常有限。在加拿大,尽管慢性乙型肝炎占全球肝癌病例的 56%,但在接受调查的 1061 名成年人中,只有 31% 的人将慢性乙型肝炎视为高癌症风险。近 90% 的受访者不知道或对慢性乙型肝炎知之甚少,45% 的加拿大成年人表示他们从未接受过检测,因为他们没有考虑过这样做或不认为自己有风险。该文章强调了初级保健机构中慢性乙型肝炎检测正常化的重要性,类似于艾滋病毒和结核病检测,并提出了一些策略,例如在例行就诊期间提供检测、教育社区和减少耻辱感。世界肝炎联盟首席执行官卡里·詹姆斯 (Cary James) 强调需要开展宣传活动和常规检测来弥补这些差距,特别是在乙型肝炎资金不断减少的高收入国家。

news.content_title: Bepirovirsen and the Push to Close Hepatitis B Care Gaps
news.content: This World Hepatitis Day, 3 expert hepatologists discuss bepirovirsen's functional cure data and weigh primary care against specialized centers for delivering this treatment. Nancy Reau, MD; Tatyana Kushner, MD; Kimberly Brown, MD World Hepatitis Day, observed July 28, arrives this year alongside new phase 3 data on bepirovirsen, an investigational antisense oligonucleotide positioned as a potential functional cure for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) .1 CHB affects more than 240 million people worldwide and accounts for over half of global liver cancer cases, underscoring the diagnostic and treatment gaps World Hepatitis Day is meant to spotlight.1 GSK recently reported a pooled functional cure rate of 19% among bepirovirsen recipients across the B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 trials (233 of 1220 vs 0 of 614 with placebo; P <.001 in both trials).Results were presented at the European Association for the Study of the Liver congress and published in the New England Journal of Medicine on May 28, 2026. The rate rose to 26% among participants with baseline hepatitis B surface antigen levels of 1000 IU/mL or lower, a subgroup representing approximately 45% of diagnosed CHB cases globally.1 The US Food and Drug Administration has granted the therapy Priority Review and Breakthrough Therapy designation, with a PDUFA target action date of October 26, 2026.1 Despite that progress, most CHB cases in the United States remain undiagnosed, and most patients who are diagnosed and treatment-eligible are not receiving therapy. A new drug with a novel mechanism could drive renewed screening efforts. It also raises questions about where treatment will be delivered, since many patients, particularly within Asian communities, are managed in primary care rather than hepatology practices. Liver Lineup: Bepirovirsen and the Push Toward Functional Cure in Hepatitis B On a recent episode of Liver Lineup: Updates & Unfiltered Insights , Tatyana Kushner, MD, joined hosts Nancy Reau, MD, and Kimberly Brown, MD, to discuss how care delivery models may need to adapt to accommodate bepirovirsen. Together, they weighed primary care providers' existing experience managing complex hepatitis B populations against the added monitoring demands, including surveillance for ALT flares, that come with a new mechanism of action. Kimberly Brown: Many patients with hepatitis B are not in our practices, right? They're in primary care practices, especially the Asian population. There are several primary care practitioners in the community that manage large groups of hepatitis B patients. Do you think that's an appropriate setting? That's where a lot of these patients are sitting, they're not really in hepatology practices always. What are we thinking about the uptake in those practices? Tatyana Kushner: That's a really good point, and I think probably the first step will have to be to increase education and awareness that this treatment is on the horizon, and I do think that GSK, the company that makes bepirovirsen, are really thinking actively about how to do that and how to target their educational efforts. So the first step, I think, will be to make everyone aware that it's on the horizon. Then, in terms of where this treatment is administered, again, it will depend on how it looks in terms of monitoring, but to me it seems more that there will be some specialized centers that are able to take this on and treat with this medication. Would it be a situation where those patients who are currently being followed in primary care actually have to be referred to a specialized center just to complete this treatment course, and then referred back to their primary care for ongoing treatment after? I'm just not convinced that with all the nuances with this treatment, that that will be able to be done in routine primary care settings, but I think we'll have to see. Nancy Reau: I think that not all PCPs are the same. For a lot of our Asian patients, their hepatitis B is followed by a primary care provider that has a lot of expertise in hepatitis B, and our primary care doctors do hard things, right? They can give GLP-1s, which are injection therapy. They might be using cholesterol medicines that are alternative options. They might be giving bisphosphonates that are IV. I mean, there's lots of things that PCPs do that are inconvenient. I think a primary care provider that has a large population of hepatitis B might really be excited about another drug, because it affects a majority of the patients. I think PCPs that have a handful of hepatitis B patients, where liver cancer surveillance, and even antiviral therapy may not be done the way that our guidance would suggest, those patients are probably going to have to be linked to a more specialized center. I also think that just the approval of a new drug and a new mechanism of action will have an uptick in screening. One of the biggest issues in the US is the majority of hepatitis B patients are still not diagnosed, and of those that are diagnosed and appropriate for treatment, the majority are not on any treatment. So, hopefully, it'll shift a little more towards screening and standard of care. Tatyana Kushner: Yeah, that is a really good point, and I think that it will depend on the care setting, and whether they have many patients who have hepatitis B, then why not take this on. But again, there’s the question of ALT flares. I mean, I'm scared when I see these high ALT elevations, how about a primary care doctor who is seeing all these hepatitis B carriers, or you know, patients that are relatively well controlled, who hasn't really dealt with ALT flares in this setting. I think it's those kinds of situations that may be a little bit distinct in a specialized setting versus primary care, but I agree that if they have a lot of hepatitis B experience, they may want to be able to be the ones that are offering this to their patients. Editors’ note: Relevant disclosures for Reau include AbbVie, Gilead, Salix, Arbutus, and VIR. Relevant disclosures for Brown include Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals, Gilead, Salix, Intercept, Ipsen, and Madrigal. Relevant disclosures for Kushner include Gilead, Abbvie, GSK, Ipsen, Mirum, and Madrigal. news.content_original: This World Hepatitis Day, 3 expert hepatologists discuss bepirovirsen's functional cure data and weigh primary care against specialized centers for delivering this treatment. Nancy Reau, MD; Tatyana Kushner, MD; Kimberly Brown, MD World Hepatitis Day, observed July 28, arrives this year alongside new phase 3 data on bepirovirsen, an investigational antisense oligonucleotide positioned as a potential functional cure for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) .1 CHB affects more than 240 million people worldwide and accounts for over half of global liver cancer cases, underscoring the diagnostic and treatment gaps World Hepatitis Day is meant to spotlight.1 GSK recently reported a pooled functional cure rate of 19% among bepirovirsen recipients across the B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 trials (233 of 1220 vs 0 of 614 with placebo; P <.001 in both trials).Results were presented at the European Association for the Study of the Liver congress and published in the New England Journal of Medicine on May 28, 2026. The rate rose to 26% among participants with baseline hepatitis B surface antigen levels of 1000 IU/mL or lower, a subgroup representing approximately 45% of diagnosed CHB cases globally.1 The US Food and Drug Administration has granted the therapy Priority Review and Breakthrough Therapy designation, with a PDUFA target action date of October 26, 2026.1 Despite that progress, most CHB cases in the United States remain undiagnosed, and most patients who are diagnosed and treatment-eligible are not receiving therapy. A new drug with a novel mechanism could drive renewed screening efforts. It also raises questions about where treatment will be delivered, since many patients, particularly within Asian communities, are managed in primary care rather than hepatology practices. Liver Lineup: Bepirovirsen and the Push Toward Functional Cure in Hepatitis B On a recent episode of Liver Lineup: Updates & Unfiltered Insights , Tatyana Kushner, MD, joined hosts Nancy Reau, MD, and Kimberly Brown, MD, to discuss how care delivery models may need to adapt to accommodate bepirovirsen. Together, they weighed primary care providers' existing experience managing complex hepatitis B populations against the added monitoring demands, including surveillance for ALT flares, that come with a new mechanism of action. Kimberly Brown: Many patients with hepatitis B are not in our practices, right? They're in primary care practices, especially the Asian population. There are several primary care practitioners in the community that manage large groups of hepatitis B patients. Do you think that's an appropriate setting? That's where a lot of these patients are sitting, they're not really in hepatology practices always. What are we thinking about the uptake in those practices? Tatyana Kushner: That's a really good point, and I think probably the first step will have to be to increase education and awareness that this treatment is on the horizon, and I do think that GSK, the company that makes bepirovirsen, are really thinking actively about how to do that and how to target their educational efforts. So the first step, I think, will be to make everyone aware that it's on the horizon. Then, in terms of where this treatment is administered, again, it will depend on how it looks in terms of monitoring, but to me it seems more that there will be some specialized centers that are able to take this on and treat with this medication. Would it be a situation where those patients who are currently being followed in primary care actually have to be referred to a specialized center just to complete this treatment course, and then referred back to their primary care for ongoing treatment after? I'm just not convinced that with all the nuances with this treatment, that that will be able to be done in routine primary care settings, but I think we'll have to see. Nancy Reau: I think that not all PCPs are the same. For a lot of our Asian patients, their hepatitis B is followed by a primary care provider that has a lot of expertise in hepatitis B, and our primary care doctors do hard things, right? They can give GLP-1s, which are injection therapy. They might be using cholesterol medicines that are alternative options. They might be giving bisphosphonates that are IV. I mean, there's lots of things that PCPs do that are inconvenient. I think a primary care provider that has a large population of hepatitis B might really be excited about another drug, because it affects a majority of the patients. I think PCPs that have a handful of hepatitis B patients, where liver cancer surveillance, and even antiviral therapy may not be done the way that our guidance would suggest, those patients are probably going to have to be linked to a more specialized center. I also think that just the approval of a new drug and a new mechanism of action will have an uptick in screening. One of the biggest issues in the US is the majority of hepatitis B patients are still not diagnosed, and of those that are diagnosed and appropriate for treatment, the majority are not on any treatment. So, hopefully, it'll shift a little more towards screening and standard of care. Tatyana Kushner: Yeah, that is a really good point, and I think that it will depend on the care setting, and whether they have many patients who have hepatitis B, then why not take this on. But again, there’s the question of ALT flares. I mean, I'm scared when I see these high ALT elevations, how about a primary care doctor who is seeing all these hepatitis B carriers, or you know, patients that are relatively well controlled, who hasn't really dealt with ALT flares in this setting. I think it's those kinds of situations that may be a little bit distinct in a specialized setting versus primary care, but I agree that if they have a lot of hepatitis B experience, they may want to be able to be the ones that are offering this to their patients. Editors’ note: Relevant disclosures for Reau include AbbVie, Gilead, Salix, Arbutus, and VIR. Relevant disclosures for Brown include Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals, Gilead, Salix, Intercept, Ipsen, and Madrigal. Relevant disclosures for Kushner include Gilead, Abbvie, GSK, Ipsen, Mirum, and Madrigal. news.source_body_en: On World Hepatitis Day 2026, expert hepatologists discussed bepirovirsen, a promising new therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) with a 19% functional cure rate in phase 3 trials, rising to 26% in a key subgroup. With over 240 million people affected globally and most cases undiagnosed or untreated, the drug's novel mechanism could drive renewed screening efforts. However, questions remain about care delivery: while many patients, especially in Asian communities, are managed in primary care, experts debate whether specialized centers are better equipped to handle monitoring demands like ALT flares. GSK has secured FDA Priority Review and Breakthrough Therapy designation, with an October 2026 decision date. The discussion highlights the need for education and adaptable care models to address persistent gaps in hepatitis B management.

news.content_title: Hepatitis B vs Hepatitis C: Which viral liver infection is more dangerous?
news.content: Hepatitis B vs Hepatitis C: Which viral liver infection is more dangerous? Hepatitis B Vs Hepatitis C: How Are These Viral Infections Different? Read on to know how different these two viral infections are and what symptoms the body actually shows when it is infected with the virus. Medically Verified By: Dr. Deepak Ganga P Hepatitis B vs Hepatitis C: Which viral liver infection is more dangerous? Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C are two of the most common viral infections affecting the liver. Both hepatitis can lead to chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer. Hepatitis B and hepatitis C have many similarities, which raises the question of which is more harmful. Both infections have serious consequences to health, but they differ in the way of transmission and development of the disease. Hepatitis B vs Hepatitis C: What Are The Key Differences? In an exclusive interaction with TheHealthSite.com, Dr. Deepak Ganga P, Senior Consultant - Medical Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Interventional Endoscopy, KIMS Hospitals, Mahadevapura, Bengaluru, explained why it is important to understand both types of hepatitis, and how they differ from each other. Hepatitis B is common as hepatitis C and is caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV). It is transmitted when blood and infected body fluids come in contact with people. Transmission can occur from mother to child during childbirth, due to unprotected sex, sharing of needles or unsafe medical procedures. In adults hepatitis B could resolve without treatment. Hepatitis C is an infection leading to by a virus called hepatitis C virus (HCV) and is transmitted mainly through infected blood. Nowadays, the greatest number of people get the infection through contributing blood or sharing needles. Sexual transmission is uncommon, similar to hepatitis B, although it might take place at times. HCV is more commonly transitioned into chronic infection when compared to HBV, which in the majority of cases leads to chronic liver disease and thus to serious conditions in the absence of treatment. Hepatitis B vs Hepatitis C: How Different Are The Symptoms? As for the symptoms of the disease, both infections are silent because many infected people do not present any symptoms for many years. When symptoms occur, fatigue or lack of appetite may appear and nausea, discomfort in the abdomen as well as dark urine and yellow skin may also occur. The question arises as to which is riskier. The hepatitis B vaccine has proven very effective and has played an immense role in reducing infection rates. But even though chronic hepatitis B has not been cured, the use of antiviral treatment can help to hold the virus in check and avoid adverse outcomes. In contrast to hepatitis B, hepatitis C does not have any vaccine, generically making its prevention even more important. Luckily, the progress of science and medicine brought some revolutionary DAAs (direct-acting antivirals), which allow curing hepatitis C in over 95% of cases under the right situations and at the right time. Why Is Treating Hepatitis Important? Still, doctors insist that instead of true comparison of the two types of infection, it is far more important to understand that both can be fatal if left ignored. The detection of either type can be achieved through blood tests thus, people with considerable risk factors need to get tested and cure if necessary. You may like to read Getting a vaccine for hepatitis B, employing safe sex practices, and staying away from sharing needles or personal belongings that may contact blood. Safe medical practices help in lowering the likelihood of infection. With early diagnosis, appropriate medical care, and treatment, it is possible for many hepatitis B or C patients to have otherwise normal and productive lives with low chances of liver complications arising. Do not take this as medical advice, and ensure that you are checked by a proper doctor before encouraging any home remedies for managing the condition. news.content: Treat all Hepatitis B cases immediately to save lives If the Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is suppressed, the risk of transmission to the family and close contacts is negligible. Published on: Jul 28, 2026, 08:36:41 IST By SK Sarin Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link Two infections had comparable global death tolls in 2024: Tuberculosis (TB) killed 1.23 million, and Hepatitis B 1.1 million, while HIV-related illnesses killed 630,000. For Hepatitis B, the toll was 17% more than it was in 2015. In 2021, Hepatitis B consumed an estimated 21.5 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). Nearly 30-35 million in India suffer from this infection and about 5-10 million may eventually die due to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Yet public recognition, political attention, and funding are strikingly unequal, with Hepatitis B receiving very low quanta of each. No wonder, the world, including India will miss the 2030 WHO targets — instead of the 90% targeted, diagnosing merely 3-15%, and the 80% targeted, treating just 5% of infected. Less than a million are receiving treatment despite a large National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) since 2018. If the Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is suppressed, the risk of transmission to the family and close contacts is negligible. (Pexel) The problem is the medical profession itself. Unlike HIV and Hepatitis C (another liver virus causing cirrhosis and cancer) where every patient receives treatment, for Hepatitis B , medical algorithms demand high viral load, abnormal liver enzymes, liver scarring or fibrosis for getting treatment. Patients who fail to qualify must undergo repeated blood tests, viral-DNA measurements, fibrosis assessments, specialist consultations throughout life. As the virus remains silent for years, patients are often told to wait. This becomes a painful ordeal. The system spends money monitoring the virus, refusing to suppress it, while hurting the psyche of the infected. These recommendations originate mostly in western countries where tests and drugs are expensive. Also Read: Who should get tested for hepatitis? Gastroenterologist shares screening guidelines even if you have no symptoms A ray of hope, though, came last month. The new Asian guidelines on Hepatitis B, recommend “Treat All” rather than “Treat Select”. The generic antivirals are low-cost in retail and also available under the NHVCP, and should cost less than ₹ 1,000 for a daily pill for a month. Pills taken daily can effectively suppress the virus for life with minimal adverse event and resistance. After China, India houses the largest number of Hepatitis B subjects. India should adopt a “test once, treat early and monitor simply” approach. Broadening treatment would not only reduce the DALY burden but also lower the several-fold higher cost of treatment for cirrhosis, cancer and transplantation for patients. India must adopt the Asian guidelines and reverse the expensive misallocation of scarce health resources in testing to treatment. Ghana showed that using conventional criteria made about only 10% of patients eligible, but by treating anyone with detectable Hepatitis B DNA raised eligibility to 87%. Health systems should stop spending scarce resources proving that people with Hepatitis B are not yet sick enough to treat. India will save substantially by screening households of infected and treating most, and early. Developing its own national cost-effectiveness model, using Indian prices, disease progression, adherence, cancer costs, productivity, and procurement rates would help. If the Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is suppressed, the risk of transmission to the family and close contacts is negligible. One’s own risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer falls markedly. This changes expenditure from high-cost rescue care for a small number of very sick patients to low-cost prevention distributed across a much larger population. We, the doctors, present the hurdle: Physicians must stop being gatekeepers who certify when Hepatitis B has caused enough damage. They should become preventers who ensure it never does. Also Read: Worried about Hepatitis B and C? Gastroenterologist Dr Shubham Vatsya explains facts that every family should know We need to do a lot to reduce the stigma of Hepatitis B, very often associated with HIV. We need to join the EMPATHY (Empowering People Against Hepatitis) campaign. Physicians should explicitly state in certificates and counselling that ordinary social and workplace contact does not spread HBV. They should challenge inappropriate employment exclusion, refusal of procedures, and marriage-related misinformation. Treating the infected should be strongly supplemented by protecting the next generation. HBV vaccine given at birth and followed by week 6, 10 and 14 can protect nearly every newborn. India has taken good strides in this direction, but much more can be done. Every adult should also get this most economical and effective vaccine. July 28 is World Hepatitis Day; this time, it is being observed with the theme “Hepatitis: Let us break it down”. We need to break the barriers, starting with social acceptance and dignity for the infected, change in attitude of the physicians to “Treat Most”, and supportive policies of treatment and funding by the government. Every single Hepatitis B death is a reminder of our inept policies and delayed judgement. Act now, and, collectively to eliminate hepatitis B. SK Sarin is professor of eminence, Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences, New Delhi. The author calls for physicians to change from being gatekeepers to preventers and for government policies to support broader treatment access.
