news.content_title: Mission aims to support 1.5 lakh Hepatitis B screenings nationwide through a physician-led awareness and screening initiative
news.content: Mission aims to support 1.5 lakh Hepatitis B screenings nationwide through a physician-led awareness and screening initiative The campaign also unveiled the World's Largest Liver Model, created using Hepatitis B antigen test kit covers that will be used to screen 1.5 lakh individuals, serving as a public installation to reinforce the importance of timely screening and diagnosis. Written By: Sponsored | Published : July 30, 2026 12:08 PM IST Share Mumbai, July XX 2026 : Despite advances in diagnosis and treatment, Hepatitis B continues to remain one of India's under-recognised public health challenges. India accounts for nearly 12% of the global Hepatitis B burden , with an estimated 4 crore people living with chronic Hepatitis B infection . Yet only around 3% are diagnosed , while less than 1% receive appropriate treatment , leavingmillions unaware of their infection and at risk of developing serious liver disease. Recognising the importance of early diagnosis, Cipla has joined hands with Indian National Association for the Study of the Liver (INASL) to continue Mission Defeat Hepatitis . A nationwide initiative aims to raise awareness, encourage early diagnosis, and at expand access to Hepatitis B screening across India . As part of this year's World Hepatitis Day observance, more than 5,000 doctors across the country have joined the initiative to support 1.5 lakh Hepatitis B screenings. Recognising the scale of this physician-led awareness and screening drive, the campaign has also earned an entry into the International Book of Records. This marks the first phase of a larger effort to facilitate more than 2.5 lakh screenings through over 8,500 screening camps nationwide. The event brought together healthcare professionals, liver disease experts and Cipla leadership to reinforce the need for timely Hepatitis B screening and diagnosis. The campaign also unveiled the World's Largest Liver Model, created using Hepatitis B antigen test kit covers that will be used to screen 1.5 lakh individuals, serving as a public installation to reinforce the importance of timely screening and diagnosis. Commenting on the initiative, Dr. Jaideep Gogtay, Chief Medical Officer, Cipla Limited, said, "Hepatitis B remains one of the under-diagnosed public health challenges in India. While effective therapies are available, millions continue to live with the infection without knowing their status. We believe awareness and early diagnosis are the first steps towards changing this reality. Through Mission Defeat Hepatitis, we are bringing together the medical fraternity, scientific bodies and communities to encourage timely screening and help people access appropriate care. Our vision is simple, to ensure that every individual at risk has the opportunity to know their Hepatitis B status. Because only when we diagnose earlier can we truly change the course of the disease." Speaking on the initiative, Prof. Dr. Ajay Duseja, HOD PGI & INASL Secretary General, said, "The Indian National Association for the Study of the Liver (INASL) is a non-profit organisation committed to advancing the discipline of hepatology in India. Early diagnosis remains one of the most effective interventions in Hepatitis B management. Mission Defeat Hepatitis provides an opportunity for healthcare professionals across the country to work towards a shared goal of increasing awareness, encouraging screening and connecting patients to appropriate care. Together, we can make meaningful progress in reducing the burden of Hepatitis B in India." Dr. Amit Mandot (Director Dept of Hepatology & LICU: Gleneagles Hospital, Mumbai): " Early diagnosis is a cornerstone of effective Hepatitis B management, enabling timely intervention and significantly reducing the risk of advanced liver disease. Mission Defeat Hepatitis serves as a platform to unite healthcare professionals in a collective effort to enhance awareness, encourage screening, and facilitate early linkage to care. We at INASL & Gleneagles Hospital have active partnership in this initiative, particularly its support for screening programs and awareness-building activities that help drive early detection within the community. Through such collaborative efforts, we can accelerate progress toward reducing the burden of Hepatitis B in India and improving patient outcomes." Dr. Bipin Chevale, CEO of Gleneagles Hospital, " Hepatitis B continues to be one of the underdiagnosed liver diseases in India, despite being preventable and treatable with timely intervention. Our association with Mission Defeat Hepatitis Campaign highlights our commitment to promoting early screening and increasing public awareness, as early diagnosis remains the key to preventing serious liver complications. Through our experienced multidisciplinary team and state-of-the-art healthcare infrastructure, we strive to ensure that every patient has access to quality care, while contributing to the larger goal of reducing the burden of Hepatitis B in our communities, " Disclaimer: This article is from the Brand Desk. news.content: StartSportSwitzerlandInternationalFootballPeopleMyTechLifestyleNews HealthWHO Calls for Greater Efforts in the Fight Against Hepatitis B and CNearly 300 million people are chronically infected with the hepatitis B or C viruses. There is a vaccine against hepatitis B. (File photo)KeystoneIn the fight against hepatitis, the World Health Organization (WHO) is calling for more research, more testing and treatment, and stronger political commitment. According to the WHO, 287 million people worldwide are living with chronic hepatitis B or chronic hepatitis C.Keystone-SDA28.07.2026, 04:43These two diseases—which are not related—are caused by viruses that are transmitted primarily through blood. The liver inflammation resulting from the infection can lead to serious long-term complications such as cirrhosis and liver cancer.Hepatitis B poses the greater burden: About 240 million people worldwide live with it, and 1.1 million die from hepatitis B each year—more than twice as many as from malaria. About 240,000 people die from hepatitis C each year. And although the vast majority of hepatitis C cases have been curable since 2015, only about 20 percent of those affected have been treated since then, as the WHO pointed out on Tuesday on the occasion of World Hepatitis Day.According to the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH), approximately 0.5 to 0.7 percent of the population in Switzerland is chronically infected with the hepatitis B virus. The number of reported cases of acute hepatitis B in Switzerland is showing a downward trend, the FOPH states on its website. The number of people infected with hepatitis C is also declining. Depending on the estimate, 0.1 to 0.4 percent of the population in Switzerland is chronically infected with the hepatitis C virus.Vaccination RecommendedThe WHO recommends routine hepatitis B testing for pregnant women—and vaccination for babies born to infected women immediately after birth. The FOPH also recommends vaccination at an early age. Vaccination is likewise recommended for at-risk groups of all ages. The federal government cites healthcare workers and people who use drugs as examples. There is no vaccine against hepatitis C.A study this spring gave hepatitis experts cause for hope: For the first time, a Chinese team succeeded in achieving a functional cure in some hepatitis B patients using combination therapy. A functional cure means that the viral load is below the detection limit—even though the virus could multiply again later, for example, if the immune system is compromised.Found an error?Report nowMore About this TopicArgentinaMilei Wants to Deport Foreigners for "Hate Speech"MID Games of ChanceFour lucky winners will receive 2,222 francs per month for five yearsUnbelievable Fraud in ItalyMan Builds an Amphitheater—and Rips Off Tourists for YearsFranceA warehouse containing old military ammunition explodes during a forest fireMost Read1French Farmhouse: George and Amal Clooney Evacuated Due to Wildfire2Hiker falls 80 meters into stream bed - Rega rescue takes hours3FIFA expert Tognoni: “Gianni Infantino is pursuing a two-pronged strategy”4Heat Wave Hits with Full Force – Everything You Need to Know Right Now5Ikea goods appear illegally in a shopping center in PyongyangWHO Calls for Greater Efforts in the Fight Against Hepatitis B and CWe Care About Your PrivacyWe and our 229 partners store and/or access information on a device, such as unique IDs in cookies to process personal data. analysis.brief_en: The WHO is urging increased global efforts to combat hepatitis B and C, which affect nearly 300 million people worldwide. Hepatitis B poses a greater burden, with 240 million cases and 1.1 million annual deaths, compared to 240,000 deaths from hepatitis C. While hepatitis C is largely curable, only 20% of patients have received treatment since 2015. In Switzerland, chronic hepatitis B affects 0.5-0.7% of the population, with acute cases declining. The WHO recommends routine testing for pregnant women and vaccination for newborns of infected mothers, while the FOPH advocates early vaccination and for at-risk groups. A recent study offers hope for a functional cure for hepatitis B through combination therapy.

Tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) appears to be a safer option for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) than tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), with similar efficacy, according to study findings published in BMC Infectious Diseases. Researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize head-to-head data comparing TAF and TDF for chronic HBV infection. The analysis included 4 randomized controlled trials with a total of 1960 patients. Mean patient age ranged from 38 to 56 years within the trials, which all assessed endpoints at 48 weeks. Two trials included only hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg)-negative patients, with the other 2 including both HBeAg-negative and -positive patients. The primary outcome was the suppression of HBV DNA to less than 15 to 29 IU/mL, which did not differ significantly between the TAF and TDF groups in a random-effects model (risk ratio [RR], 1.00; 95% CI, 0.96-1.05; P =.82). These insights underscore the need for ongoing investigation to optimize treatment strategies for CHB [chronic hepatitis B] patients. Patients who received TAF, however, were more likely to have a normalization of alanine transaminase levels (RR, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.16-1.64; P =.0002) and had smaller reductions in bone mineral density measured at the hip (mean difference [MD], 1.44; 95% CI, 0.98-1.91; P <.00001) and spine (MD, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.42-2.44; P <.00001) compared with those who received TDF. Receipt of TAF was also associated with a lesser increase in serum creatinine concentration (MD, -0.02; 95% CI, -0.03 to -0.01; P <.00001) and smaller drop in estimated glomerular filtration rate (MD, 3.55; 95% CI, 2.97-4.14; P <.00001). Patients who received TAF vs TDF experienced worse outcomes in regard to low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels, being approximately 5-fold more likely to have levels greater than 190 to 300 mg/dL (RR, 4.95; 95% CI, 1.21-20.29; P =.03). The researchers cautioned that “the estimate is uncertain due to a few events and wide confidence intervals.” Study limitations include the inability to explore additional outcomes related to bone health and kidney function or additional lipid parameters beyond LDL cholesterol, the relatively small number of trials, the high risk of bias in 2 of the trials, heterogeneity in clinical characteristics across trials, the inability to examine potential differences in longer-term outcomes due to follow-up lasting only 48 weeks, and the fact that all 4 trials were sponsored by the manufacturer of both medications. According to the researchers, “These insights underscore the need for ongoing investigation to optimize treatment strategies for CHB [chronic hepatitis B] patients.” References: Dar MS, Ovais H, Khan AW, et al. The analysis, based on 4 trials with 1960 patients, highlights TAF's potential to optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing organ toxicity, though limitations include trial sponsorship and short follow-up duration.

news.content_title: Short-Chain Fatty, Bile Acids Signal in Chronic Hep B
news.content: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Science 31 Jul 2026 12:30 am AEST Date Time Xia & He Publishing Inc. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global challenge. Current therapies suppress HBV but rarely achieve functional cure (sustained HBsAg loss). Emerging gut‐liver axis evidence shows that microbial metabolites—short‐chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids (BAs)—modulate HBV replication and immunity. Butyrate suppresses HBV via HDAC inhibition and cccDNA epigenetic remodelling. SCFAs may enhance antiviral immunity but can also reinforce tolerance. BAs signal through FXR, TGR5, and the HBV entry receptor NTCP, forming a dual‐effect hub. Early studies suggest FXR agonists combined with PegIFN‐α may reduce HBsAg. This review proposes biomarker‐guided stratification and multi‐target strategies to improve functional cure rates. Introduction CHB affects ~254 million people, causing ~1.1 million annual deaths. Functional cure (HBsAg loss with undetectable HBV DNA) is rarely achieved with current NAs or PegIFN‐α (HBsAg clearance rates: 1.4–5.1% for NAs, 2.1–20% for PegIFN‐α). Most patients need lifelong therapy. The gut‐liver axis offers new targets via SCFAs and BAs, which regulate viral replication and hepatic immunity. SCFAs in HBV Infection SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) are produced by colonic fermentation. Butyrate directly suppresses HBV in cell lines via HDAC inhibition, remodelling cccDNA chromatin, and may enhance p53 activity. However, effective in vitro concentrations are millimolar, far exceeding physiological micromolar levels—a key translational gap. Immunologically, SCFAs act through GPR41/43 and GPR109A: they can promote antiviral responses (T cells, NK cells, macrophages) and reduce hepatic stellate cell inflammation. Conversely, they may promote Treg differentiation and IL‐10/TGF‐β, reinforcing immune tolerance—particularly concerning in the immune‐tolerant phase. The net effect depends on disease stage and immune context. Bile Acids in HBV Infection Primary BAs are synthesised from cholesterol and converted to secondary BAs by gut microbiota. They signal through FXR (nuclear) and TGR5 (membrane). FXR has dual effects: physiological activation enhances HBV transcription (proviral), but sustained high‐dose FXR agonists may downregulate FXR and suppress HBV via negative feedback. FXR activation also downregulates NTCP, the HBV entry receptor, potentially reducing de novo infection. TGR5 activation reduces inflammation via cAMP/NF‐κB but has no direct antiviral effect; dual FXR/TGR5 agonists like INT‐767 may block viral entry by binding preS1. NTCP is both the BA uptake transporter and essential HBV receptor; its inhibition (e.g., bulevirtide) blocks entry but risks BA homeostasis disruption. SCFA‐BA Synergies and Therapeutic Strategies BAs can suppress butyrate‐producing bacteria, further reducing SCFAs in advanced fibrosis; SCFAs regulate BA synthesis via the FXR‐FGF19 axis and strengthen gut barrier. Thus, a self‐reinforcing cycle of dysbiosis, BA dysregulation, and SCFA depletion is a key therapeutic target. Therapeutic approaches include direct SCFA supplementation, prebiotics/probiotics/FMT, and FXR agonists (vonafexor, ASC42) in early trials. Combinations with PegIFN‐α may improve HBsAg decline. Future strategies include intestinal‐targeted FXR modulators and dual FXR/TGR5 agents. Metabolic‐immune combinations (e.g., SCFA prodrug + NA + immunotherapy) may target multiple mechanisms. Patient stratification by disease phase and gut microbiota/metabolic profiles is essential. Limitations and Risks Evidence is predominantly preclinical; clinical data are scarce and small‐scale. Dosing gaps exist (in vitro vs. physiological concentrations). FXR agonists may cause pruritus, dyslipidaemia, and cholestasis; SCFAs may cause GI effects or promote tolerance; probiotics/FMT carry infection risks. Long‐term viral adaptation and durability of HBsAg loss are unknown. Conclusion and Outlook Targeting SCFA and BA pathways offers a promising frontier for CHB. SCFAs suppress HBV epigenetically and modulate immunity; BAs influence viral transcription (FXR), entry (NTCP), and inflammation (TGR5). These axes are complementary, supporting multi‐target combination strategies. Future work should focus on multi‐omics profiling for stratification, humanised models, rigorous RCTs, and next‐generation delivery platforms. With careful development, metabolic‐immune combinations may improve functional cure rates and patient outcomes. Current therapies suppress HBV but rarely achieve functional cure (sustained HBsAg loss). Emerging gut‐liver axis evidence shows that microbial metabolites—short‐chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids (BAs)—modulate HBV replication and immunity. Butyrate suppresses HBV via HDAC inhibition and cccDNA epigenetic remodelling. SCFAs may enhance antiviral immunity but can also reinforce tolerance. BAs signal through FXR, TGR5, and the HBV entry receptor NTCP, forming a dual‐effect hub. Early studies suggest FXR agonists combined with PegIFN‐α may reduce HBsAg. This review proposes biomarker‐guided stratification and multi‐target strategies to improve functional cure rates. Introduction CHB affects ~254 million people, causing ~1.1 million annual deaths. Functional cure (HBsAg loss with undetectable HBV DNA) is rarely achieved with current NAs or PegIFN‐α (HBsAg clearance rates: 1.4–5.1% for NAs, 2.1–20% for PegIFN‐α). Most patients need lifelong therapy. The gut‐liver axis offers new targets via SCFAs and BAs, which regulate viral replication and hepatic immunity. SCFAs in HBV Infection SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) are produced by colonic fermentation. Butyrate directly suppresses HBV in cell lines via HDAC inhibition, remodelling cccDNA chromatin, and may enhance p53 activity. However, effective in vitro concentrations are millimolar, far exceeding physiological micromolar levels—a key translational gap. Immunologically, SCFAs act through GPR41/43 and GPR109A: they can promote antiviral responses (T cells, NK cells, macrophages) and reduce hepatic stellate cell inflammation. Conversely, they may promote Treg differentiation and IL‐10/TGF‐β, reinforcing immune tolerance—particularly concerning in the immune‐tolerant phase. The net effect depends on disease stage and immune context. Bile Acids in HBV Infection Primary BAs are synthesised from cholesterol and converted to secondary BAs by gut microbiota. They signal through FXR (nuclear) and TGR5 (membrane). FXR has dual effects: physiological activation enhances HBV transcription (proviral), but sustained high‐dose FXR agonists may downregulate FXR and suppress HBV via negative feedback. FXR activation also downregulates NTCP, the HBV entry receptor, potentially reducing de novo infection. TGR5 activation reduces inflammation via cAMP/NF‐κB but has no direct antiviral effect; dual FXR/TGR5 agonists like INT‐767 may block viral entry by binding preS1. NTCP is both the BA uptake transporter and essential HBV receptor; its inhibition (e.g., bulevirtide) blocks entry but risks BA homeostasis disruption. SCFA‐BA Synergies and Therapeutic Strategies BAs can suppress butyrate‐producing bacteria, further reducing SCFAs in advanced fibrosis; SCFAs regulate BA synthesis via the FXR‐FGF19 axis and strengthen gut barrier. Thus, a self‐reinforcing cycle of dysbiosis, BA dysregulation, and SCFA depletion is a key therapeutic target. Therapeutic approaches include direct SCFA supplementation, prebiotics/probiotics/FMT, and FXR agonists (vonafexor, ASC42) in early trials. Combinations with PegIFN‐α may improve HBsAg decline. Future strategies include intestinal‐targeted FXR modulators and dual FXR/TGR5 agents. Metabolic‐immune combinations (e.g., SCFA prodrug + NA + immunotherapy) may target multiple mechanisms. Patient stratification by disease phase and gut microbiota/metabolic profiles is essential. Limitations and Risks Evidence is predominantly preclinical; clinical data are scarce and small‐scale. Dosing gaps exist (in vitro vs. physiological concentrations). FXR agonists may cause pruritus, dyslipidaemia, and cholestasis; SCFAs may cause GI effects or promote tolerance; probiotics/FMT carry infection risks. Long‐term viral adaptation and durability of HBsAg loss are unknown. Conclusion and Outlook Targeting SCFA and BA pathways offers a promising frontier for CHB. SCFAs suppress HBV epigenetically and modulate immunity; BAs influence viral transcription (FXR), entry (NTCP), and inflammation (TGR5). These axes are complementary, supporting multi‐target combination strategies. Future work should focus on multi‐omics profiling for stratification, humanised models, rigorous RCTs, and next‐generation delivery platforms. With careful development, metabolic‐immune combinations may improve functional cure rates and patient outcomes. analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-30. Event date: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: ~254 million people with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
analysis.event: Scientific review published in the Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology on the role of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids (BAs) in chronic hepatitis B infection. The review discusses emerging gut-liver axis evidence and proposes biomarker-guided stratification and multi-target strategies to improve functional cure rates.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: CHB causes ~1.1 million annual deaths. Current therapies achieve functional cure (HBsAg loss) in only 1.4–20% of patients. The review highlights the potential of SCFAs and BAs as therapeutic targets but notes evidence is predominantly preclinical with limited clinical data.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The review proposes therapeutic strategies including direct SCFA supplementation, prebiotics/probiotics/FMT, and FXR agonists in early trials. Limitations include scarce clinical data, dosing gaps between in vitro and physiological concentrations, potential side effects (pruritus, dyslipidaemia, GI effects), and unknown long-term viral adaptation and durability of HBsAg loss.

analysis.brief_en: A recent review in the Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology explores the gut-liver axis in chronic hepatitis B (CHB), highlighting the role of microbial metabolites—short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids (BAs)—in modulating HBV replication and immunity. SCFAs like butyrate suppress HBV via HDAC inhibition and epigenetic remodelling, while bile acids signal through FXR and TGR5, influencing viral transcription and entry. The review notes that current therapies rarely achieve functional cure, with only 1.4–20% of patients achieving HBsAg loss. Emerging strategies include SCFA supplementation, FXR agonists, and combination therapies with PegIFN-α, though clinical data remains limited. The authors emphasize the need for patient stratification and multi-target approaches to improve outcomes, while acknowledging risks such as dosing gaps and potential side effects.

news.content_zh: 《临床与转化肝病学杂志》最近发表的一篇评论探讨了 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 中的肠肝轴,强调了微生物代谢物——短链脂肪酸 (SCFA) 和胆汁酸 (BA)——在调节 HBV 复制和免疫中的作用。丁酸盐等 SCFA 通过 HDAC 抑制和表观遗传重塑来抑制 HBV,而胆汁酸则通过 FXR 和 TGR5 发出信号,影响病毒转录和进入​​。该综述指出,目前的治疗很少能达到 功能性治愈,只有 1.4-20% 的患者实现 HBsAg 消失。新兴策略包括 SCFA 补充剂、FXR 激动剂和 PegIFN-α 联合疗法,但临床数据仍然有限。作者强调需要对患者进行分层和多目标方法来改善结果,同时承认剂量差距和潜在副作用等风险。

Discover Saudi Leading Edge Powering Progress Experience Brazil Italy – Heritage & Horizons Poland Untold Costa Rica Beyond Business Saadiyat Cultural District My Tokyo Kerala Tourism Dubai Global Digital Economy Hub Turkmenistan - Our story Endless Discovery Expo 2025 Osaka, Kansai, Japan Services Weather Bulletin Messaging apps Widgets & Services Online Language Courses Newsletter Newsletters Events Events Podcasts Videos Africanews Loader Find Us ADVERTISEMENT Advertisement Health Health news Europe set to miss 2030 hepatitis elimination targets, health agency warns Europe to miss 2030 hepatitis elimination targets. - Copyright Cleared/Canva Copyright Cleared/Canva By Marta Iraola Iribarren Published on 28/07/2026 - 11:55 GMT+2 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Despite years of progress, the ECDC says Europe is to miss its 2030 goal to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat, as gaps in child vaccination and inadequate reduction measures are seen across Europe. Despite progress over the last few years in preventing hepatitis B and C, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warns the region is off track to meet the 2030 elimination targets. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT “No one should die from a disease that is preventable, diagnosable and treatable, yet millions of Europeans are living with chronic hepatitis B or C infections – often without knowing it – which can lead to severe long-term consequences such as liver failure or liver cancer,” said Bruno Ciancio, Head of Unit for Directly Transmitted and Vaccine-Preventable Diseases at ECDC. Hepatitis B and C are transmitted through infected blood or bodily fluids and are among the leading causes of chronic liver disease. While acute hepatitis B infections have been falling steadily since 2006, driven by long-standing vaccination and prevention efforts, an estimated five million people in Europe are still living with chronic hepatitis B or C, and around 60,000 die every year from liver disease linked to these infections, according to the ECDC. Among people younger than 25 years, the proportion of acute hepatitis B cases fell from 11% in 2015 to 8% in 2024, reflecting the impact of childhood vaccination programmes and other prevention measures. Routine screening for hepatitis B in pregnancy is also well established across all 30 European Union and European Economic Area countries, helping to bring down transmission of the virus from mother to child to below 2%, the ECDC said. Ciancio noted that effective control solutions are already in place. Those include vaccination to prevent hepatitis B, harm reduction and infection control initiatives to reduce transmission, testing to identify infections early, and treatments that can cure hepatitis C and control hepatitis B. Related Millions in Europe unknowingly living with hepatitis, health authorities warn Gaps across Europe However, experts have identified gaps in routine childhood vaccination. Only a minority of countries have reached the World Health Organization (WHO) target of fully vaccinating 95% of children against hepatitis B, with others even reporting a decline in coverage in recent years. Harm reduction measures — such as opioid agonist treatment and the provision of sterile needles and syringes — are effective in limiting transmission of hepatitis C. Still, coverage remains inadequate, and only seven countries meet the WHO target for distributing sterile injection equipment to people who inject drugs. “Our collective challenge is to ensure that these life-saving interventions are accessible to everyone who needs them,” Ciancio said. Sexual transmission remains a major route of hepatitis B transmission. For hepatitis C, most cases are linked to injecting drug use and sex between men. Yet, the ECDC noted that specific prevention efforts targeting sexual transmission of hepatitis across different populations have not been systematically monitored across countries. news.content_title: Hawaiʻi tackles liver cancer by taking on hepatitis
news.content: HONOLULU (KHON2) — A healthy liver works quietly every day, but diseases like viral hepatitis can do the same. Many people in Hawaiʻi do not know they have an infection until serious liver damage has already begun. That's why education, testing and vaccination have remained a key part of Hawaiʻi's effort to prevent hepatitis and reduce the risk of liver disease. World Hepatitis Day is observed every year on July 28. The day has been a means for raising awareness about viral hepatitis and encouraging people to learn about prevention, testing and treatment. In Hawaiʻi, the Department of Health has created a campaign and provided information to help residents understand how hepatitis spreads, who may be at risk and what steps can help prevent infection. Hawaiʻi is one of the states with the highest rates of liver cancer, and viral hepatitis B and hepatitis C are the leading causes. Viral hepatitis is a group of viruses that attack the liver. The most common types in Hawaiʻi are hepatitis A, hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Hepatitis A usually causes a short-term illness. It spreads through close personal contact or by consuming contaminated food or water. A vaccination offers protection, and good handwashing helps prevent the spread of the virus. Hepatitis B can begin as a short-term infection and may become a long-term illness. Chronic hepatitis B can lead to liver damage, cirrhosis, liver cancer and death. The virus spreads through infected blood, semen or other body fluids; and it can be passed from an infected mother to her baby during birth, through sex with an infected partner, by sharing needles or through contact with infected blood. The Department of Health noted that hepatitis B does not spread through food or water, sharing eating utensils, breastfeeding, hugging, kissing, holding hands, coughing or sneezing. They also said there is no vaccine for hepatitis C. The Department of Health identified vaccination as the best way to prevent hepatitis A and hepatitis B. The hepatitis A vaccine is given as two doses six months apart. The hepatitis B vaccine is given as a series of three shots over six months. Completing the full series provides long term protection. They also encouraged hepatitis B testing for people in several groups that include Household and sexual contacts of people with hepatitis B. Anyone who may have been exposed to hepatitis B should contact a health care provider immediately. The DOH said treatment soon after exposure may help prevent infection. The DOH also has been supporting education through Hep Free Hawaiʻi . The partnership has brought together doctors, community organizations and advocates to increase awareness, encourage testing and vaccination and connect people with medical care and support. Since the campaign began in 2011, Hep Free Hawaiʻi has held events across the state to promote hepatitis awareness and testing. On World Hepatitis Day in 2011, the DOH said a group tested 140 people and identified 10 who were positive for hepatitis and did not know they were infected. You can click here to access the DOH's page on viral hepatitis, here for their page on hepatitis B and here for hepatitis A. The DOH encouraged residents to learn about hepatitis, stay up to date on recommended vaccinations and talk with a health care provider about testing when appropriate. news.content_original: HONOLULU (KHON2) — A healthy liver works quietly every day, but diseases like viral hepatitis can do the same. Many people in Hawaiʻi do not know they have an infection until serious liver damage has already begun. That's why education, testing and vaccination have remained a key part of Hawaiʻi's effort to prevent hepatitis and reduce the risk of liver disease. World Hepatitis Day is observed every year on July 28. The day has been a means for raising awareness about viral hepatitis and encouraging people to learn about prevention, testing and treatment. In Hawaiʻi, the Department of Health has created a campaign and provided information to help residents understand how hepatitis spreads, who may be at risk and what steps can help prevent infection. Hawaiʻi is one of the states with the highest rates of liver cancer, and viral hepatitis B and hepatitis C are the leading causes. Viral hepatitis is a group of viruses that attack the liver. The most common types in Hawaiʻi are hepatitis A, hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Hepatitis A usually causes a short-term illness. It spreads through close personal contact or by consuming contaminated food or water. A vaccination offers protection, and good handwashing helps prevent the spread of the virus. Hepatitis B can begin as a short-term infection and may become a long-term illness. Chronic hepatitis B can lead to liver damage, cirrhosis, liver cancer and death. The virus spreads through infected blood, semen or other body fluids; and it can be passed from an infected mother to her baby during birth, through sex with an infected partner, by sharing needles or through contact with infected blood. The Department of Health noted that hepatitis B does not spread through food or water, sharing eating utensils, breastfeeding, hugging, kissing, holding hands, coughing or sneezing. They also said there is no vaccine for hepatitis C. The Department of Health identified vaccination as the best way to prevent hepatitis A and hepatitis B. The hepatitis A vaccine is given as two doses six months apart. The hepatitis B vaccine is given as a series of three shots over six months. Completing the full series provides long term protection. They also encouraged hepatitis B testing for people in several groups that include Household and sexual contacts of people with hepatitis B. Anyone who may have been exposed to hepatitis B should contact a health care provider immediately. The DOH said treatment soon after exposure may help prevent infection. The DOH also has been supporting education through Hep Free Hawaiʻi . The partnership has brought together doctors, community organizations and advocates to increase awareness, encourage testing and vaccination and connect people with medical care and support. Since the campaign began in 2011, Hep Free Hawaiʻi has held events across the state to promote hepatitis awareness and testing. On World Hepatitis Day in 2011, the DOH said a group tested 140 people and identified 10 who were positive for hepatitis and did not know they were infected. You can click here to access the DOH's page on viral hepatitis, here for their page on hepatitis B and here for hepatitis A. The DOH encouraged residents to learn about hepatitis, stay up to date on recommended vaccinations and talk with a health care provider about testing when appropriate. Igbiti said poor health-seeking behaviour remains one of the biggest challenges in the fight against hepatitis, as many people fail to seek medical attention when symptoms first appear. According to him, hepatitis has two stages; acute and chronic, with the acute stage occurring within the first six months of infection. “The acute phase commonly presents with fever, body weakness and joint pains, which many people simply assume is malaria. As a result, they do not go to the hospital for proper testing,” he said. He explained that although many people recover from the acute phase, some progress to chronic hepatitis without realising it because the symptoms subside. RELATED NEWS Expert Warns Against Neglecting One’s Health Over 1,000 Persons Benefit From Free Medical Outreach Nigeria, Development Partners Push Sustainable Growth ln Pharmaceutical Industry “The danger is that by the time many people discover they have hepatitis, the disease may have already caused serious liver damage, including cirrhosis or liver cancer. Our goal is not to diagnose hepatitis when someone already has liver cancer or cirrhosis. We want to detect it early enough to prevent those complications,” he said. Igbiti identified inadequate awareness, limited access to screening in rural communities and vaccine hesitancy as other major factors driving the burden of hepatitis in Nigeria. He noted that many awareness campaigns and screening exercises are concentrated in urban areas, leaving people in hard-to-reach communities without access to testing and preventive services. “Our outreaches need to go beyond the cities. People in remote communities are not being reached, and even when they are, some are reluctant to take blood tests or receive vaccines because of misconceptions,” he said. The gastroenterologist urged governments and development partners to intensify public education, expand community-based screening and strengthen vaccination campaigns to improve hepatitis prevention and early detection. He explained that the federal government introduced the Hepatitis B vaccine into the National Programme on Immunisation in 2004, ensuring routine vaccination for newborns. However, he noted that many adults born before then remain unprotected and should be screened and vaccinated. “Most people born before 2004 did not benefit from routine vaccination at birth. All adults should know their hepatitis status, and those who are eligible should be vaccinated,” he said. Igbiti added that completing the recommended three-dose Hepatitis B vaccination regimen provides protection for more than 30 years, while immunity can be monitored through antibody titre testing, particularly among healthcare workers and other high-risk groups. He further noted that although there is no vaccine for Hepatitis C, the disease is curable if detected early, stressing that regular follow-up for infected persons is essential to prevent liver damage and improve treatment outcomes. news.content: How early screening saved Hong Kong woman from her family’s liver cancer fate Health authorities renew call for early hepatitis B screening, citing 40 per cent of 410,000 patients in city being unaware of condition Hongkonger Ms Lam has long known she is carrying a ticking time bomb after her mother and grandmother died of liver cancer. Her mother was completely asymptomatic until a late-stage diagnosis left no option for surgery. “I knew I carried the hepatitis B virus when I was in my twenties and had since then undergone regular health check-ups to manage the bomb,” the woman in her fifties recalled. Her regular checks were only disrupted during the Covid-19 pandemic. When she returned for a check-up in 2024, tests showed a surging viral load and a liver tumour despite her not feeling any pain. Caught early, the tumour was successfully removed, and she was back on her feet just days after the operation. Hepatitis B rarely behaves that way. It can quietly damage the liver for years, sometimes decades, without causing symptoms. By the time many people learn they have it, the disease may have already progressed to cirrhosis, liver failure or even liver cancer. That silent nature is one reason India continues to carry one of the world's largest hepatitis B burdens. For most families, these numbers feel distant until someone close is diagnosed. By then, the disease may already have caused serious damage.2/7The frightening part is that hepatitis B can stay silent for decadesMany people imagine that a serious liver disease would announce itself with obvious warning signs. Unfortunately, hepatitis B rarely does."India has the second highest hepatitis-B burden globally with an estimated 40–50 million chronic carriers. Hepatitis-B is one of the viruses causing chronic hepatitis and in the long run leading to end-stage liver disease or cirrhosis and liver cancer. As a liver transplant surgeon who deals with end stages of this virus, we see devastating results, cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma)," said Dr Ankur Garg, Group Director, Liver Transplant & GI Surgery, Paras Health, Gurgaon.That explains why specialists often refer to hepatitis B as a silent infection.According to Dr Garg, the virus can quietly inflame the liver for years without causing noticeable symptoms."Hepatitis-B is often in a silent carrier state and does not lead to any clinical symptoms or concerns for years or decades. The virus causes slow, silent chronic inflammation in the liver. By the time symptoms occur in the form of jaundice, fatigue, lethargy or abdominal swelling, the liver is heavily scarred (cirrhosis). This is the time surgeons often meet such patients for the first time, and it becomes shocking for the patient and family to hear that liver transplant is the only option now."That is one reason liver specialists emphasise screening even when a person feels completely healthy.3/7Why India's high burden is a family matter, not just an individual oneOne of the biggest misconceptions is that hepatitis B spreads only through risky behaviour. In reality, many infections in India happen much closer to home."It is frequently passed down in families. It spreads via blood and bodily fluids. The most common form of transmission is either mother to child (vertical transmission), this being the most common in India when a pregnant mother passes this to her newborn child. The second is household spread (horizontal transmission). The virus can survive outside the body for up to a week. Sharing razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers or even minor cuts and scrapes within the household can easily transmit the virus to other members," explained Dr Garg.That changes how people should think about the infection.A hepatitis B diagnosis in one family member should encourage other close relatives to get tested. It is not about creating fear. It is about protecting those who may have been unknowingly exposed over the years.The WHO notes that hepatitis B is not spread through hugging, sharing food, coughing or casual social contact, which is why people living with the infection should never face stigma.4/7The good news: This is one of the few cancers that can often be preventedNot every health story comes with a hopeful ending. This one does.Hepatitis B is preventable through vaccination, and preventing infection also reduces the risk of future liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.India introduced the hepatitis B vaccine into its Universal Immunisation Programme in phases beginning in 2002 and later expanded coverage across the country. Children born after widespread implementation are far more likely to have received protection than many adults who were born earlier."It is preventable and highly treatable but rarely curable. Vaccination has a very good bearing, 100% protection. India introduced vaccination against hepatitis-B in universal immunisation in 2002. However, millions born before 2002 are often not vaccinated."5/7Testing positive does not mean your life is overA hepatitis B diagnosis often creates panic because many people immediately think of liver failure. Doctors say that is no longer the reality for most patients.Modern antiviral medicines can keep the virus under control for years, reducing the risk of severe liver damage when taken under medical supervision."If someone tests positive, just taking one pill, for example entecavir or tenofovir, a day will keep this virus silent for more than 99% of the cases, although resistant cases do exist. However, these medicines will not cure the infection; they will keep the virus suppressed," said Dr Garg.That distinction matters. Treatment suppresses the virus and helps protect the liver, but regular follow-up with a liver specialist remains essential.6/7One simple blood test today could change your futurePerhaps the most powerful message from liver transplant surgeons is also the simplest. Do not wait for symptoms. By the time symptoms appear, the liver may already have suffered years of silent damage.Dr Garg recommends a straightforward approach, "Because of India's high burden, transplant surgeons and hepatologists recommend a simple, proactive rule of thumb: Get a simple HBsAg blood test once. If you are negative, ensure you are vaccinated. If you are positive, don't panic, regular monitoring with a doctor can ensure you stay perfectly healthy and never have to see a transplant surgeon in an operating room."For many people, that single test may bring reassurance. For others, it could detect an infection early enough to prevent irreversible liver disease.Sometimes the most important health decisions are not the dramatic ones. They are the quiet, preventive steps taken long before illness ever announces itself.7/7Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Ankur Garg, Group Director Liver Transplant & GI Surgery, Paras Health, Gurgaon. supplementary_news.content_title: Chronic Hepatitis B Affects Millions Worldwide – So Why Do People Know So Little About It?
supplementary_news.content: Chronic hepatitis B is not something most people think about in their day-to-day lives.1 But, globally, it remains a major health issue – and one that health leaders say is not improving fast enough.2 Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus, which can increase the risk of developing severe liver damage (cirrhosis) and liver cancer.3 People can become infected with the hepatitis B virus through exposure to infected blood and other bodily fluids.2 Most people do not experience any symptoms when initially infected with the hepatitis B virus, and the infection can go unnoticed for many years.2˒3 It is estimated that approximately 240 million people are living with chronic hepatitis B globally.2˒3 Yet despite the burden, the World Health Organization (WHO) states that efforts to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health threat by 2030 are currently off track.2 While tools like vaccinations, testing and treatment already exist, progress has not kept pace with what is possible.2 Against that backdrop, a new global online survey commissioned and funded by GSK and conducted among 5,000 general public adults across five countries suggests that one of the biggest challenges may be something much simpler: awareness.1 Despite affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide,2 chronic hepatitis B remains out of sight for many.1 More than eight in 10 adults surveyed say they were either unaware of chronic hepatitis or knew very little about it.1 The lack of awareness goes beyond simply not recognising the disease name. Many people are unclear on basic facts – from how the virus is prevented (such as through vaccination, and reducing exposure to blood and other bodily fluids that may carry the hepatitis B virus3) and if treatment is available, to how it impacts long-term health.1 One of the most striking findings from the survey is the gap between what is known medically about chronic hepatitis B and how it is perceived by the public.1 Chronic hepatitis B is a leading cause of liver cancer, estimated to be the cause of around half of liver cancer cases globally.2˒4 Yet only approximately one in three people in the GSK survey considered it to be a high-risk factor.1 By comparison, far more people associated lifestyle and environmental risk factors like smoking, alcohol use, obesity and air pollution with cancer.1 Even among those who are aware of a link between chronic hepatitis B and liver cancer, the scale of the risk is often underestimated. On average, the adults surveyed thought chronic hepatitis B accounted for around a quarter of liver cancer cases, significantly lower than current global estimates. Low awareness does not just affect what people know. It also shapes how they think and what they do. Around three in four adults surveyed said they had never been tested for hepatitis B.1 Among adults who have never been tested, the leading barriers are simply never having considered it and not thinking they were at risk – not active refusal.1 When something isn't widely discussed and commonly understood, it can be harder to place in a personal context. What makes this issue more striking is that chronic hepatitis B is a disease we know a great deal about and can manage. Vaccination, testing and treatment for hepatitis B are well established.1 Yet globally, outcomes are not improving at the pace expected, with low treatment coverage and delayed diagnosis still contributing to rising numbers of deaths.1 The WHO's latest assessment suggests that the gap today is less about whether solutions exist, and more about how consistently they are used in practice, and how much priority is given to addressing the condition by healthcare decision makers, including policymakers. Closing that gap may depend, in part, on making the condition feel more visible and more relevant to people's lives.1 Chronic hepatitis B is too often overlooked, with consequences that can be serious for individuals, families and communities.1˒2 Greater awareness can help change that. Breaking the chain starts by breaking the silence. By talking more openly, understanding whether testing may be relevant, and knowing how to help protect yourself and others, we can take an important first step. Because when something becomes part of the conversation, it becomes easier to recognise when it matters. Talk. Test. Protect. supplementary_news.content_title: Benue records 193 Hepatitis B cases among pregnant women, moves to curb spread
supplementary_news.content: Vanguard News Home News Top Stories E-editions Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns ALLURE Search for: Home News Top Stories E-editions Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns ALLURE Home News E-Editions Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns Allure Home » News » Benue records 193 Hepatitis B cases among pregnant women, moves to curb spread News Follow us on Google July 28, 2026 Benue records 193 Hepatitis B cases among pregnant women, moves to curb spread Layer 1 By Peter Duru, Makurdi The Benue state government has disclosed that 193 pregnant women tested positive for Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) in 2025, raising concerns over the continued burden of viral hepatitis in the state despite ongoing efforts to eliminate the disease. The Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr. Paul Ogwuche, made the disclosure during the commemoration of the 2026 World Hepatitis Day, themed “Hepatitis: Let’s Break It Down.” He said the state had stepped up surveillance, screening and treatment to reduce infections and prevent mother-to-child transmission. According to him, 35,508 pregnant women were screened for Hepatitis B in 2025, with 193 confirmed positive, while studies conducted in Benue showed that the prevalence of Hepatitis B stood at eight percent and Hepatitis C at one percent. He said, “In Benue State in 2025, 35,508 pregnant women were tested for HBV, while 193 were infected. We are also working with the Federal Ministry of Health to provide prophylactic treatment for pregnant women living with HBV in order to eliminate mother-to-child transmission.” The Commissioner explained that the state had keyed into the Federal Government’s Project 365 initiative, which seeks to eliminate Hepatitis C and halt Hepatitis B transmission by 2030 through expanded screening, diagnosis and treatment services. He said hepatitis care would be integrated into primary healthcare and maternal health services across the state, while outreach programmes would be conducted in all 23 Local Government Areas, LGA, to increase testing and referrals. Dr. Ogwuche warned that viral hepatitis remained a major public health challenge in Nigeria, revealing that more than 20 million Nigerians are living with the infection, comprising about 18.2 million cases of Hepatitis B and 2.5 million cases of Hepatitis C. He lamented that more than 90 percent of infected persons were unaware of their status because the disease often presents symptoms similar to malaria, allowing it to progress undetected to liver cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer. “The scale of this silent epidemic in Nigeria is nothing short of staggering. Over 90 percent of those infected remain undiagnosed and continue to unknowingly transmit the virus to others, including their children,” he said.Related NewsRotary district calls for collective action against hepatitisWorld Hepatitis Day: 28 million people in Eastern Mediterranean living with hepatitis - WHOLagos Govt expands free hepatitis screening The Commissioner also referenced the World Health Organisation’s 2026 Global Hepatitis Report, which estimated that 287 million people globally were living with chronic Hepatitis B or C in 2024, while the two infections caused 1.34 million deaths during the year. He, however, noted that global progress in vaccination and treatment had reduced new Hepatitis B infections and Hepatitis C-related deaths, stressing that the disease could be eliminated if governments sustained investments in prevention, testing and treatment. Dr. Ogwuche urged residents of the state to get tested, receive the Hepatitis B vaccine if eligible, and seek prompt treatment where necessary, insisting that achieving the 2030 elimination target would require collective action from government, healthcare workers, development partners, the media and the public. “The tools to eliminate viral hepatitis already exist. What we need now is commitment to break the barriers that prevent people from accessing testing, vaccination and treatment,” he said. supplementary_news.content: EditionININUSGCCEnglishEnglishहिन्दीमराठीಕನ್ನಡதமிழ்বাংলাമലയാളംతెలుగుગુજરાતીWeatherSign InTOIHealthVideosCityMetro CitiesmumbaidelhibengaluruHyderabadkolkatachennaiOther CitiesCityCrime Newsagraagartalaahmedabadajmeramaravatiamritsarbareillybhubaneswarbhopalchandigarhchhatrapati sambhajinagarcoimbatorecuttackdehradunerodefaridabadghaziabadgoagurgaonguwahatihubballiimphalindoreitanagarjaipurjammujamshedpurjodhpurkanpurkochikohimakolhapurkozhikodeludhianalucknowmaduraimangalurumeerutmumbai regionmysurunagpurnashiknavi mumbainoidapatnaprayagrajpuducherrypuneraipurrajkotranchithanesalemshillongshimlasrinagarsurattrichythiruvananthapuramudaipurvadodaravaranasivijayawadavisakhapatnamphotosWeb StoriesIndiafeaturedGadgets NowUrban SafetyMaharashtraDelhiKarnatakaTelanganaWest BengalTamil NaduAndhra PradeshUttar PradeshGujaratRajasthanPunjabOdishaMadhya PradeshHaryanaTripuraUttarakhandBiharKeralaAssamArunachal PradeshManipurChhattisgarhJammu KashmirNagalandJharkhandMeghalayaHimachal PradeshWeb StoriesDigital ArrestOperation SindoorCancel PatriarchyLets D StressWorldBusinessTechGadgets NowCricketSportsEntertainmentAstroTOI WomenTVEducationLife & StyleWeb SeriesTimes EvokePhotosBlogseconomyTOI ExclusiveCelebrationsTOI GamesToday's ePaperLiveNewsHealth NewsMillions of Indians may be living with hepatitis B without knowing it: A liver transplant surgeon explains why the silent virus is so dangerousMillions of Indians may be living with hepatitis B without knowing it: A liver transplant surgeon explains why the silent virus is so dangerousAadya Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Jul 25, 2026, 23:33 ISTShareAA+Text SizeSmallMediumLargeFollow us 1/7India has one of the highest hepatitis B burdens globallyMost people worry about illnesses that arrive with obvious warning signs, a high fever, severe pain or sudden weakness. Hepatitis B rarely behaves that way. It can quietly damage the liver for years, sometimes decades, without causing symptoms. By the time many people learn they have it, the disease may have already progressed to cirrhosis, liver failure or even liver cancer. That silent nature is one reason India continues to carry one of the world's largest hepatitis B burdens. For most families, these numbers feel distant until someone close is diagnosed. By then, the disease may already have caused serious damage.2/7The frightening part is that hepatitis B can stay silent for decadesMany people imagine that a serious liver disease would announce itself with obvious warning signs. Unfortunately, hepatitis B rarely does."India has the second highest hepatitis-B burden globally with an estimated 40–50 million chronic carriers. Hepatitis-B is one of the viruses causing chronic hepatitis and in the long run leading to end-stage liver disease or cirrhosis and liver cancer. As a liver transplant surgeon who deals with end stages of this virus, we see devastating results, cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma)," said Dr Ankur Garg, Group Director, Liver Transplant & GI Surgery, Paras Health, Gurgaon.That explains why specialists often refer to hepatitis B as a silent infection.According to Dr Garg, the virus can quietly inflame the liver for years without causing noticeable symptoms."Hepatitis-B is often in a silent carrier state and does not lead to any clinical symptoms or concerns for years or decades. The virus causes slow, silent chronic inflammation in the liver. By the time symptoms occur in the form of jaundice, fatigue, lethargy or abdominal swelling, the liver is heavily scarred (cirrhosis). This is the time surgeons often meet such patients for the first time, and it becomes shocking for the patient and family to hear that liver transplant is the only option now."That is one reason liver specialists emphasise screening even when a person feels completely healthy.3/7Why India's high burden is a family matter, not just an individual oneOne of the biggest misconceptions is that hepatitis B spreads only through risky behaviour. In reality, many infections in India happen much closer to home."It is frequently passed down in families. It spreads via blood and bodily fluids. The most common form of transmission is either mother to child (vertical transmission), this being the most common in India when a pregnant mother passes this to her newborn child. The second is household spread (horizontal transmission). The virus can survive outside the body for up to a week. Sharing razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers or even minor cuts and scrapes within the household can easily transmit the virus to other members," explained Dr Garg.That changes how people should think about the infection.A hepatitis B diagnosis in one family member should encourage other close relatives to get tested. It is not about creating fear. It is about protecting those who may have been unknowingly exposed over the years.The WHO notes that hepatitis B is not spread through hugging, sharing food, coughing or casual social contact, which is why people living with the infection should never face stigma.4/7The good news: This is one of the few cancers that can often be preventedNot every health story comes with a hopeful ending. This one does.Hepatitis B is preventable through vaccination, and preventing infection also reduces the risk of future liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.India introduced the hepatitis B vaccine into its Universal Immunisation Programme in phases beginning in 2002 and later expanded coverage across the country. Children born after widespread implementation are far more likely to have received protection than many adults who were born earlier."It is preventable and highly treatable but rarely curable. Vaccination has a very good bearing, 100% protection. India introduced vaccination against hepatitis-B in universal immunisation in 2002. However, millions born before 2002 are often not vaccinated."5/7Testing positive does not mean your life is overA hepatitis B diagnosis often creates panic because many people immediately think of liver failure. Doctors say that is no longer the reality for most patients.Modern antiviral medicines can keep the virus under control for years, reducing the risk of severe liver damage when taken under medical supervision."If someone tests positive, just taking one pill, for example entecavir or tenofovir, a day will keep this virus silent for more than 99% of the cases, although resistant cases do exist. However, these medicines will not cure the infection; they will keep the virus suppressed," said Dr Garg.That distinction matters. Treatment suppresses the virus and helps protect the liver, but regular follow-up with a liver specialist remains essential.6/7One simple blood test today could change your futurePerhaps the most powerful message from liver transplant surgeons is also the simplest. Do not wait for symptoms. By the time symptoms appear, the liver may already have suffered years of silent damage.Dr Garg recommends a straightforward approach, "Because of India's high burden, transplant surgeons and hepatologists recommend a simple, proactive rule of thumb: Get a simple HBsAg blood test once. If you are negative, ensure you are vaccinated. If you are positive, don't panic, regular monitoring with a doctor can ensure you stay perfectly healthy and never have to see a transplant surgeon in an operating room."For many people, that single test may bring reassurance. For others, it could detect an infection early enough to prevent irreversible liver disease.Sometimes the most important health decisions are not the dramatic ones. They are the quiet, preventive steps taken long before illness ever announces itself.7/7Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Ankur Garg, Group Director Liver Transplant & GI Surgery, Paras Health, Gurgaon. New survey reveals Canadians underestimate chronic hepatitis B and its link to liver cancer CNW Group Tue, 28 July 2026 at 7:00 am GMT-4 6 min read GSK -2.16% GSK -2.16% Nearly 9 in 10 Canadians have little to no awareness of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) Only 31% rank CHB as a high cancer risk, revealing a significant gap between perception and reality Just 14% report to have been tested for CHB, yet CHB causes 56%2 of liver cancer cases and affects over 262,000 in Canada3 MISSISSAUGA, ON, July 28, 2026 /CNW/ -- GSK plc (LSE: GSK) (NYSE: GSK) today released new data insights from a global survey marking World Hepatitis Day. The global survey, funded and commissioned by GSK, revealed major gaps in public awareness of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in Canada, with many adults underestimating the role of CHB in liver cancer.1 GSK logo World Hepatitis Day is observed annually on July 28 to raise awareness of hepatitis and to encourage action and engagement. In Canada 1,061 adults aged 18–54+ took part in the global online survey conducted by Ipsos of approximately 5,000 respondents across Japan, Taiwan, China, Germany and Canada. CHB, a long-term viral infection, affects 262,000 people in Canada.3 It often goes undetected for years because many people have few or no symptoms, but over time it can lead to serious liver damage, including cirrhosis and liver cancer.4 Vaccination can help prevent hepatitis B,4 and greater awareness of its long-term health risks can support earlier diagnosis, testing and ongoing monitoring. The survey findings underscore the need for improved public health education on CHB, as low awareness and misconceptions about the cancer risk continue to hinder testing and early detection1. Public understanding of CHB in Canada remains strikingly low.Only 31% of Canadians rated CHB a high cancer risk (significantly lower than regular alcohol use or obesity), while nearly 9 in 10 say they are unaware or know very little about CHB, which is the leading cause of liver cancer,5 accounting for up to 56% of all liver cancer cases globally.2 Lack of awareness of CHB extends to personal risk and testing.Many Canadians lack basic knowledge of CHB and its long-term health risks: 11% say they have never heard of the virus, and only 8% of respondents believe they are likely to contract CHB. In addition, 45% of Canadian adults admit they have never been tested for hepatitis B because they haven't considered doing so or do not think they are at risk. Among those at higher risk, nearly half of respondents say they do not intend to get tested, suggesting that higher risk alone may not be enough to prompt action and that stigma and misconceptions may be discouraging people from seeking testing and care Recognition of prevention and protection options is also limited.Misconceptions about prevention and care are widespread: 55% of Canadians incorrectly believe there is no treatment for CHB and about 3 in 4 are unaware that vaccination can help protect against it. Story continues The findings are consistent with the updated Canadian Guidelines for the Management of Chronic Hepatitis B that emphasize universal screening, universal infant vaccination across all provinces and territories, and expanded treatment recommendations, including broader eligibility criteria.6 As a result, more people living with CHB may be considered for treatment. Individuals with chronic hepatitis B may wish to speak with their healthcare provider about what these changes could mean for their own care. "The data underscores a simple reality: people don't ask for a hepatitis B test when they don't know they're at risk. Most Canadians assume that if a test is important, it will be offered as part of their routine health care. Too often, that isn't happening for hepatitis B. This World Hepatitis Day, the theme is 'Let's break it down.' That means breaking down the barriers that leave people undiagnosed for years and putting in place policies to offer one-time hepatitis B screening to all adults and hepatitis B vaccination for all infants so people are identified early, connected to care and protected from the serious consequences of chronic hepatitis B, including liver cancer," said Jennifer van Gennip Executive Director, Action Hepatitis Canada. "The survey reveals a troubling disconnect: chronic hepatitis B carries serious long-term health risks, yet many Canadians do not recognize it as a concern. Awareness, understanding and education are critical. Informed conversations in the clinic are often the starting point for testing, monitoring and ongoing care. We need clear, accessible information and more informed dialogue in clinics and communities so that Canadians can better understand their risk and work with their healthcare teams to protect their liver health," added Dr. Michelle Horn, Country Medical Director, GSK Canada The World Health Organization has set targets to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, and countries that are part of WHO and the United Nations, including Canada, have agreed to take action to help meet these goals.4 About chronic hepatitis BHepatitis B is a viral infection that can cause both acute and chronic liver disease. Chronic hepatitis B occurs when the immune system is unable to clear the virus, resulting in long-lasting infection that affects more than 240 million people worldwide3, including 262,000 in Canada3. The disease causes approximately 1.1 million deaths each year3, and accounts for approximately 56% of liver cancer cases globally.2 About the Global Chronic Hepatitis B 2026 SurveyThe global chronic hepatitis B survey is a quantitative online survey of approximately 5,000 adults aged 18-54+ from Japan (978), Taiwan (961), China (1,000), Germany (1,059) and Canada (1,061). The survey was commissioned and funded by GSK, and included 11 questions exploring awareness of CHB, perceptions of cancer risk, testing behaviour and trusted sources of health information.1 Survey results are reported as aggregated data and are intended to inform disease awareness and public health education efforts.
